speakeroldname: Mr. Walter C. Carter (St. John's West):
subtopic: MR. CARTER-ALLEGED MISLEADING ANSWER BY MINISTER OF FISHERIES RESPECTING ATLANTIC SALMON REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to raise a question of privilege arising out of information given to the House by the Minister of Fisheries on a matter within the administrative responsibilities of the government. The facts are these: On April 13, 1972, as recorded in Hansard, pages 1294 and 1295, I asked the minister if he could tell the House whether it was his intention to announce new salmon fishing regulations to become effective during the forthcoming salmon season. The minister replied that no new regulations were to be announced. The government would, he said, be repeating those made last year to make sure that the fishermen fully understood the announcement made in 1971 with regard to 1972 and future years.	-
Yesterday, Mr. Speaker, ten days later, the minister announced the closure of the commercial salmon fishery dependent on salmon runs returning to the Saint John, Miramichi and Restigouche rivers and to the south coast of Newfoundland. This closure is to commence next month and continue for about six years. This statement was made to the House on motions.
Obviously, Mr. Speaker, the scheme proposed at great length by the minister was not thought up instantaneously. It must have preceded, in its formation, his answer to my question of ten days before. It would have been quite simple for him to reply then that he preferred not to answer my question as he expected to make an important announcement respecting the salmon fishery in a few days. Instead, Sir, he chose to mislead the House.
With your approval, Sir, I wish to move, seconded by the hon. member for Gander-Twillingate (Mr. Lundrigan):
That the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections forthwith inquire into and report upon the matter of the information given by the Minister of Fisheries upon behalf of the government relating to the salmon fishing regulations in the Atlantic provinces on the 13 April, 1972, to the House and the announcement made by the minister in the House on the 24 April, 1972, respecting the closure of certain salmon runs in the Atlantic provinces to commercial fishing over a period of years.

speechtext:

subsubtopic: ATLANTIC SALMON-MOTION REQUESTING INTERNATIONAL COMMISSION FOR NORTHWEST ATLANTIC FISHERIES TO ADOPT MEASURES TO ENSURE SURVIVAL OF SPECIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to speak in support of the resolution moved by my colleague the hon. member for Fundy-Royal (Mr. Fairweather). As stated yesterday, many of us on this side of the House were surprised and concerned at the announcement made by the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Davis) which outlined the unilateral action being taken by this government to close the commercial salmon fishery in parts of Atlantic Canada. I say we were surprised, Mr. Speaker, because this action can only create further unemployment in Atlantic Canada, an area which has already suffered greatly as a result of the actions of this government.
This action, which will affect, according to the minister, some 900 commercial fishermen in Atlantic Canada certainly leaves them in grave doubt concerning their financial future. Quite frankly, I am concerned over the timing of the minister's announcement. I say this because he is well aware of the meeting to be held by ICNAF, the International Commission for the North Atlantic Fisheries in Washington in May. At this meeting there will or should be delegates from Canada, from Denmark, France, Germany, Iceland, Italy, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Roumania, Spain, the U.S.S.R., Great Britain, the U.S.A. and Japan, the 15 nations who are members of the international commission.
These countries are all members of ICNAF or the Northeastern Atlantic Fisheries Convention known as NEAFC and should all be there. Under these conventions, the North Atlantic fishing nations are pledged to co-operate in protecting and conserving the fish stocks of the North Atlantic. Surely, Mr. Speaker, the representations which have been made by Canada, by the United States of America and by other concerned countries, should have served notice on all ICNAF members that not only were our own salmon stocks in danger of extinction but that this danger applied to haddock, sole, cod, herring and many other species as well. However, today, Mr. Speaker, we are dealing with a motion concerning our salmon and salmon fishermen, and I cannot help but wonder why this government and this minister took unilateral action against our own Canadian salmon fishermen when we are so close to the date of the international meeting in Washington. Hopefully, at that meeting we can obtain an international agreement leading to the use of common sense in conserving one of our basic resources.
As was said in the House yesterday and as is well known, the Danes are the worst offenders with regard to overfishing, followed by the Norwegians and the Swedes. Ever since the whereabouts at sea of our Atlantic salmon became known in the late 1950's and the early 1960's, because United States atomic submarines went under the ice in Davis Strait between Greenland and Baffin Island, on their way to the North Pole and saw millions of salmons suspended like icicles on the bottom of icebergs and iceflows, feeding on small shrimp, the fate of the Atlantic salmon has been sealed.
In 1965, the first year of the deep sea fishery, a total of 50 metric tons was caught in Davis Strait. By 1971, the catch had risen to 2,050 metric tons, or more than 4 million pounds. The impact of this excessive fishery on Canada is great. Our angling catch is down by 50 per cent.

April 25, 1972
Survival of Atlantic Salmon
Between 1966 and 1971 it declined by 50 per cent. Of great importance is the fact that between 1967 and 1971, Canadian commercial fishing, which accounts for almost 94 per cent of the total catch, has gone down by 60 per cent. The Danes claim that this is due to normal fluctuations; however, the constant decline in this resource would indicate otherwise. The development of the northern fishery and the steady decline of salmon stocks should indicate to Canadians and to other countries that this decline is simply not a coincidence.
We, as Canadians, have suffered in other ways, Mr. Speaker. We have suffered from the overfishing by the Danes, which has led to a loss in our own commercial fishery. This has lowered the incomes of our own commercial salmon fishermen. We have lost in yet other ways.
In Atlantic Canada, we can no longerhold out the hope to tourists, whether they come from the United States or central Canada, that in Atlantic Canada they can catch salmon, the king of North Atlantic fish. The salmon was a great tourist attraction in our area, and the government's failure to act ever since the whereabouts at sea of the salmon became, known in 1964-65 has cost us quite a penny in more ways than one, Mr. Speaker.
As the situation continues to deteriorate, another problem has come strongly into focus. .Obviously, the Canadian taxpayer is subsidizing the.Danish fishing fleet, at a -time when other tax dollars are being spent'to overcome threats to salmon while they are'in Canadian waters. We [DOT] are spending our tax dollars on.pollution abatement, dam removal, surveillance and on the installation of fish ladders around natural and man-made obstacles. In addition, large amounts are being spent on continuing salmon research facilities. Since the Danes have no salmon rivers of their own, it is obvious that they are catching our salmon because without-the enormous cost that is being paid to protect and improve our rivers, there would simply be no salmon.
This government must recognize that the Atlantic salmon is a very valuable natural resource. It must point out to all nations fishing in the North Atlantic that this fish is unique. It is entirely dependent on its river of origin for survival. This, Mr. Speaker, is a characteristic that is found in very few species of fish. We should-actually, we must-take the stand, unilaterally if necessary, that ana-dromous species such as salmon belong to the country of origin. We plead with the government to take that stand and we recommend that the minister make that position known forcefully when he attends the conference, which I hope is his intention, which is to be convened in May.
It is my understanding that a ban on high seas salmon fishing has been thoroughly examined by all the governments represented in ICNAF since Canada first raised the proposition in ICNAF during the 1967 meeting. A two-thirds majority of ICNAF and NEAFC members found the ban to be justifiable in terms of the powers of the two conventions, and the ban has been in legal effect for 12 members of ICNAF since early 1970. A few governments, namely, the Danish, the Norwegian and I believe the Swedish, continue to oppose the ban. This brings into question the over-all effectiveness of these two commissions and their ability to protect adequately our declining fishing resources.

It simply does not make sense for a few nations to make virtually all of the investment required to conserve and protect the Atlantic salmon while others reap a harvest from this fishery to which they have made no significant investment. In my opinion, if the Danes or any other country continue to fish our salmon on the high seas, we shall have to consider making a charge against them on a tonnage basis for salmon resource development as long as that resource lasts. It is my understanding that the Danish government has already given Canada a token contribution to help in salmon research, which indicates that their actions are already weighing heavily on their consciences. However, we have passed the stage at which we can talk of international quotas on our salmon. Only a total ban on international salmon fishing is acceptable to Canada. Only with the co-operation of Canadian anglers, anglers from other countries, the commercial fishing industry and all other users of our rivers can the king of fish be saved.

subsubtopic: ATLANTIC SALMON-MOTION REQUESTING INTERNATIONAL COMMISSION FOR NORTHWEST ATLANTIC FISHERIES TO ADOPT MEASURES TO ENSURE SURVIVAL OF SPECIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I feel the hon. member for South Shore (Mr. Crouse) has given an excellent summary of our position regarding the Atlantic salmon situation today. I am happy to join him in saying a few words in support of the motion put forward by the hon. member for Fundy-Royal (Mr. Fairweather).
* Perhaps I should preface my remarks, particularly for the benefit of those who live on the Pacific coast of Canada where the salmon fishery is also of very great importance, by saying that when we talk about the Atlantic salmon we are talking about a different kind of fish than that usually referred to as salmon in British Columbia. I remind hon. members of the House that the fish- on the Pacific coast that is most like the Atlantic salmon .is the one we call steelhead, or the Pacific steel-head trout. -
The question we are discussing today has been brought forward in a unique way. I hope the significance of this motion, after it has been passed unanimously by this House, as I hope it will be, will not escape the international community of nations that is concerned about the North Atlantic fishery. According to my recollection, what we are doing today in dealing with fisheries matters constitutes a "first". The things that are happening in the oceans of the world are coming more to the fore. I hope that responsible ministers and representatives of Canada who will attend the forthcoming meeting of the International Commission in Washington will not only draw attention to this resolution but draw to the attention of the other members of the commission eyerything said on this subject in this House yesterday and today.
In my hand I hold the most recent issue of International Wildlife, published by the National Wildlife Federation of the United States. In it there is an article by Thor Heyerdahl which, although not referring specifically to salmon as such, is pertinent. Referring to the Atlantic ocean and his impressions on crossing, the author says:
Crossing the Atlantic on a papyrus boat, one is impressed not so much with the vastness of the ocean as by the fact that it is so very much smaller than we usually think it is ...
Although we are living in the era of moon travel, we cling to the pre-Columbian concept of an endless ocean running into the blue space of the universe. We do not admit to ourselves that the oceans are "landlocked" with all the sewers and all the refuse of the world constantly running into them, without any outlet. We have
April 25, 1972

almost destroyed Lake Erie and Lake Michigan, yet the Indians who lived on its shores centuries ago would have believed this impossible.
We hold political discussions on whether we should be permitted to dump waste inside or outside territorial waters. But there is no "territorial water" in an ocean; it is constantly rotating like a boiling pot.
As I said, that quotation does not directly refer to the situation of the Atlantic salmon, but it at least gives some picture of the body of water we are discussing when talking about a ban on the high seas fishing of salmon in the Atlantic.	. ..
The International Commission for the North Atlantic Fisheries is in many ways a rather unique organization, particularly as far as fisheries international organizations are concerned, because of the number of nations that are participating in it. I hope that the crisis which has developed in Canada with regard to the salmon fishery as a result of the minister's- announcement yesterday, will impress the members of the commission with not only its uniqueness but its weakness. I suggest that very pertinent to the forthcoming meetings in Washington to discuss the salmon question may be an analysis of the weaknesses in the operation of the commission.
While the number of nations participating in some fishing conventions for the Pacific is smaller, nevertheless in actual practice they are in some ways much more effective because of the agreement on the actual take of fish. If one has any familiarity with the operation of the International Pacific Salmon Fisheries Commission and its work in restoring very severely damaged runs of Fraser river salmon, and any knowledge of the fact that at one time the North Pacific halibut was being fished almost to the point of extinction, both of which were brought back to fisheries that yielded major sources of food, he can understand the basic weaknesses of the North Atlantic set-up which has sparked the situation which is the subject matter of-this motion.
I hope that as a result of the passage of this motion, which involves agreement that the survival of the Atlantic salmon as a species is of paramount concern and refers, to taking whatever steps are necessary to ensure such survival, there will be, some real down-to-earth discussion by members of the commission meeting in Washington that will lead to the kind of revision of the North Atlantic Fisheries Convention that is necessary if it is to be an effective operating vehicle for the preservation of the resources of the North Atlantic.

subsubtopic: ATLANTIC SALMON-MOTION REQUESTING INTERNATIONAL COMMISSION FOR NORTHWEST ATLANTIC FISHERIES TO ADOPT MEASURES TO ENSURE SURVIVAL OF SPECIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Davis) announced yesterday the radical decision which he made unilaterally regarding commercial salmon fishing in the great Saint John, Miramichi and Restigouche rivers.
In fact, the minister has banned salmon fishing for a six-year period to be determined with the fishermen themselves. This is fine and it provides enough time for a complete cycle in order sufficiently to replenish stocks in rivers so that commercial fishing may be resumed.
Survival of Atlantic Salmon	.
Over 900 fishermen will thus lose their employment and their income. The problem is extremely serious.
Mr. Speaker, the International Commission for the Northwest Atlantic Fisheries (ICNAF), of which Canada and Denmark are members, was to watch the situation. But nothing has been done and this commission has been an utter failure; meanwhile, the federal government has failed to intervene to assure the conservation of marine resources under a short- and long-term planning policy. It has done nothing essentially, although it was aware of the situation. The minister himself admitted it yesterday when he said, and I quote:
* Historically, the total mainland take accounted for approximately one-half of the over-all catch of Atlantic salmon by Canadians. This volume has been sharply reduced. It has fallen by more than 80 per cent since 1967. On the Miramichi, where escapements formerly were measured in the tens of thousands of large fish, they are now measured in the hundreds.
- Why then did the minister not foresee this, since he was aware of the situation, and why did he not act for the conservation of our resources? Why also did he not propose a sensible policy to ensure the development of those resources?
On the other hand, Danish fishermen are operating in our fishing grounds. What is the government doing? Nothing. Has it protested? Not to our knowledge. What does it intend to do? It is taking a unilateral decision and saying to the fishermen: "Commercial fishing will no longer be allowed in our waters, but compensation will be paid to you."
Mr. Speaker, a meeting will be held in Washington in May 1972 about that problem. My colleagues from the Social Credit party of Canada and myself strongly support the resolution introduced today and we encourage the minister to take an extremely firm and clear stand at the meetings of that Commission.
It is time that foreigners learn that the Canadian people believe in natural resources and intend by all possible means to protect them, especially the huge marine resources which are wasted, due to our lack of a conservation or development policy.
Mr. Speaker, Canada must again protect the runs and the minister knows it. Indeed, I would like to hear the minister, as the situation is serious, state the means which he intends to take to assure the future protection of runs.
We must, on the other hand, compensate adequately fishermen whose income is now almost wiped out.
Third, we must in Canada, in view of the length of this period during which fishing will be banned, provide assistance and retraining for these 900 fishermen, namely the breadwinners, so as to enable them to provide for their own needs. To sum it up, this new measure will create 900 more unemployed.
Mr. Speaker, this question is too important to become a matter of partisan politics. I will conclude my remarks by urging strongly the minister to take a firm stand at the meetings to be held in Washington in May, so that foreigners will realize that Canadians intend to take every possible means at their disposal to ensure the respect of international agreements.

Survival of Atlantic Salmon
Denmark had signed this treaty, but did not respect it. And salmon fishing on the high seas has contributed directly to a loss of employment for 900 individuals in the Maritimes, which is extremely serious.
I would therefore urge the minister to take an extremely firm stand in Washington in order to create awareness of what Canadians want, what they need. I ask him to see that studies are set aside and that a very explicit policy is adopted for the preservation of our resources. First of all, they must be assessed, after which a policy of short and long-term preservation and adequate operation should be adopted so that future generations do not face the same problems we have today.
If the minister and his precedessors and the government had taken the necessary action as soon as it became known that the existence of salmon was at stake, and if at that time they had insisted on observance of the treaty, we probably should not be faced with the present problem.
Mr. Speaker, I trust that the minister will take a firm stand in Washington so that, once and for all, foreigners may become aware that Canada possesses immense resources. There is no reason why in Canada, with such vast resources, some of our citizens should suffer unemployment or poverty just because of our failure to preserve our resources by adequate operation.

speakeroldname: Hon. lack Davis (Minister oi the Environment and Minister of Fisheries):
subsubtopic: ATLANTIC SALMON-MOTION REQUESTING INTERNATIONAL COMMISSION FOR NORTHWEST ATLANTIC FISHERIES TO ADOPT MEASURES TO ENSURE SURVIVAL OF SPECIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity today to second the motion put forward by the member for Fundy-Royal (Mr. Fairweather) which, in effect, condemns the harvesting of salmon on the high seas. Canada's position for 20 years, has been that the harvesting of species like salmon, which return home to spawn, should take place in or near the rivers themselves. Unless a policy of that kind is followed there is no incentive to maintain the stock, to keep the species alive, and to keep it alive and in a healthy state.
The Atlantic salmon, in marked contrast to the Pacific salmon, is now in the category of an endangered species. This is true particularly of the large Atlantic salmon which spawns in our mainland rivers, in the Maritimes and in Quebec. At one time the Atlantic salmon ran in great numbers in all of the rivers of Europe. Now, few streams see salmon returning to their numbers diminish every year. Salmon used to run in the rivers of New England, including the Hudson. They used to run up the St. Lawrence, up the Ottawa past Parliament Hill, up into Lake Ontario. They vanished from those areas decades ago.
The remaining rivers to which the large Atlantic salmon return in quantity are those of New Brunswick and Quebec. We have taken an important step in recent days by closing these fisheries. The main purpose is to ensure that the endangered species survives, and that these rivers are brought back into a condition as near as possible to that of their original state. It is possible for this to be done. It has been done with respect to rivers on the west coast of Canada. I might add that on the west coast we have been able to maintain salmon runs at or about the level of the 1920s. Now, they are actually increasing,

despite heavy fishing and industrialization. Clearly, it is possible to bring our runs back in the Atlantic region as well.
For the benefit of the hon. members from Newfoundland, most of the salmon that return to the streams of Newfoundland and Labrador are one year fish. They don't go to Greenland. The ones that do go to Greenland are two year fish from the mainland. There, they are fished in large numbers by the Scandinavians, the Danes, the Norwegians and the Faroese. The big mainland salmon are the ones which concern us most. This is why we are concentrating on the Saint John, the Miramichi and the Restigouche. This is why the Province of Quebec will have to take similar measures on some of its big rivers as well.
There has been a dramatic decline in the return of large salmon to those mainland rivers, a drop of more than 80 per cent since 1967. This cannot be allowed to continue.
There are two reasons for this decline. First, there is the greed of Scandinavian countries, principally the Danes, but also latterly the Norwegians and to some extent the Faroese. They must stop fishing on the high seas. And after they stop, we still have the problem of bringing the stocks back. We will have to interrupt our own commercial fishery at the mouths of our rivers. There is no way in which we can allow dozens of boats, each dragging a half a mile of netting behind it, to cruise backward and forward across the mouths of those rivers, and still expect these runs to come back quickly. This is why we have taken the decision, one which was discussed with the ministers of fisheries from the maritimes and Newfoundland, and with fishermen's representatives over recent weeks, to close the fishery for a period of years. We are going to pay compensation. We are going to make funds available in an amount which is greater than the recent annual earnings of commercial fishermen to those who are affected by our ban. We shall be establishing committees of fishermen and river management committees to help us bring back these stocks. We shall employ fishermen who want jobs as river guardians in the policing of the waters. We shall pay others for their gear, or make cash settlements. We will help all fishermen to participate in other fisheries as long as the ban lasts.
The main note I wish to strike is one of optimism with regard to the long term future. We intend to get these salmon runs back, and this is the only way to do it. Had we simply curtailed the length of the season, we should merely have cut the income of fishermen. Their incomes would have been cut back without compensation. Actually, the compensation which we are offering will offset the loss of income of the fishermen during the period in which they are not allowed to fish, and when the runs revive, these men will have the opportunity to go back and fish a new, much larger run of large salmon. This is an approach which the fishermen themselves prefer because they will be much better off in the short term and long term, than they would be if they were allowed to fish the salmon to extinction.
I think the behaviour of Denmark is reprehensible. We have had meetings with the Danes both within the International Commission for the North Atlantic Fisheries and bilaterally. In 1970, in the ICNAF meetings, an agreement
April 25, 1972

was reached with the Danes that they should hold the 1971 catch at their 1969 level. They were not to put more gear into the water, for example. In 1971 their catch went up by approximately 30 per cent. There are a number of reasons why this was so. My officials tell me that they used more gear and they fished more frequently. The mesh they used was finer, they improved their fishing methods. They changed over to monofilament yarn in the nets and were better informed last year-they knew more about the fishery. These are the reasons their catch went up by 30 per cent. The Danes landed more of these large salmon than all our mainland commercial fishermen combined. Obviously, we have to stop the Danes from fishing on this scale. We have to stop Norway getting into this fishery as it has done in the last few years.
I might tell the hon. member for South Shore (Mr. Crouse) that Sweden is not in this fishery. The Faroese are. Through ICNAF we must convince them, through the pressure of public opinion we must prevent them-

subsubtopic: ATLANTIC SALMON-MOTION REQUESTING INTERNATIONAL COMMISSION FOR NORTHWEST ATLANTIC FISHERIES TO ADOPT MEASURES TO ENSURE SURVIVAL OF SPECIES
speechtext: In what year?

subsubtopic: ATLANTIC SALMON-MOTION REQUESTING INTERNATIONAL COMMISSION FOR NORTHWEST ATLANTIC FISHERIES TO ADOPT MEASURES TO ENSURE SURVIVAL OF SPECIES
speechtext:
This year, 1972. From now on. The United States has, for some inexplicable reason, decided to enter into an agreement with Denmark for the Danes to phase out by December 31, 1975. Well, four years is three years too many. They have got to stop now.
As hon. members know, our next opportunity to sit across the table from the Danes is in Washington toward the end of next month. At that time 14 nations assemble, all of them nations that fish the North Atlantic. At that time, we will be talking to the Danes. Last time round the vote was 12 to 2 in our favour, but the Danes, supported by West Germany, decided to go against our resolution, the traditional Canadian resolution, to ban salmon fishing on the high seas; in other words, to limit the catching of salmon to those countries that look after their rivers. We were proposing to look after those countries that clean up and police their salmon streams, that build hatcheries and ensure their spawning grounds are kept in good condition. This has been our policy for many years; all hon. members know that. But we have not yet managed to convince the greedier nations of the world to go along with the protection of what is really an endangered species.
To give some idea of the decline of the salmon fishery, the total salmon fishery on the east coast is only about one-twentieth the size of the salmon fishery on the west coast. It has reached that condition because of man's greed, yet there are still greedy people around who want to eliminate the species altogether. At least, that is the likely effect of their actions if they are allowed to continue their current practices.
In any case, Mr. Speaker, we will be meeting the Danes in Washington along with the representatives from another dozen countries. We hope that we will be able to convince them to stop fishing this summer, not next summer or the following summer, but this summer. We have managed through FAO to arrange an international meeting, a meeting of all the world's fishing nations, in Vancouver next February. We will be talking primarily about the management of the world's fishing resources, and we
Survival of Atlantic Salmon
will be talking about salmon again. We will be underlining our case for salmon to be fished only by those countries that look after their own rivers.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I want to emphasize the fact that we have been in touch with the fishermen, and the fishermen agree with our approach. It is the only approach that will save the Atlantic salmon, and I hope that the Danes, the Norwegians and the Faroese get the message spelled out in this unanimous resolution of the House of Commons of Canada.

speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. One of the concerns of the members of this party is the loss of universality under the provisions of this bill. The second concern we have is the unworkability of the proposals before us. We realize we are in the computer age, and that calculations can be made today that a few years ago would never have been undertaken on a mass scale affecting 20 million Canadians. But even with this change, it is very probable that the bill will be unworkable because of the calculations that will have to be made in connection with the incomes of Canadian families. Incomes vary a great deal from family to family, from one year to the next year, and even within the course of one year.
A matter that gives me great concern is this: We have recently been experiencing the repercussions of the new Unemployment Insurance Act which introduced some new concepts. One was the provision of sickness benefits, while another related to the taking into account of holiday pay and severance pay. When one realizes how badly these provisions fouled up procedures and settlements that were due to people who had paid their insurance, one understands what can result from a bill such as this.
Those individuals who apply for unemployment insurance are people who have paid money into the fund. They are not asking for charity; rather they go to the unemployment insurance office to claim benefits that are due to them. I have at different times received reports from people who have made a claim for benefits but have run into difficulty, either because those administering the system have not adjusted to the changes, or because there is real difficulty in calculating benefits in certain areas. In addition, those who apply for benefits sometimes find themselves treated as mendicants, as people who are asking for a grant or a gift from the state. This should not be, but the proposals in this bill could very well put a number of people in the same position.

There is no question about it, all families will have to establish what their income was in any year in order to collect, and the responsibility will fall on them to do so. The bill reads, in part:
Where at any time during the first eleven months of a benefit year, other than the fourth month, or during the eighth month period next before that benefit year a parent
(a)	ceases to hold an office or employment previously held by
him or ceases to carry on a business previously carried on by
him, or
(b)	for any other reason suffers a loss or reduction of income, as a result of which event or occurrence it is reasonable to expect that the income of the family for the calendar year in which the event or occurrence took place or for the next following calendar year will be substantially reduced, the parents may, in such manner and within such time as are prescribed, file a statement of the estimated income of the family for the calendar year in which the event or occurrence took place, in which case the income of the family received during that part of the calendar year after the month in which the event or occurrence took place divided by the number of months in that part of that calendar year and multiplied by twelve shall be deemed to be the income of the family for the base calendar year.
If anybody was able to follow the sense of that section after the first sentence, he should stand up and take a bow. The clause provides that parents may, in such case, file a statement, but what happens if they do not? When they ask for their payments will some clerk or other person in the department say, "you did not file a statement"? Is this compulsory or is it not? Will the individual have to establish what his income may have been or is going to be? He is supposed to file a statement outlining what the reasonable expectations are for the family income for the calendar year. There are many people who have no basis upon which to make a forecast of their income. This is just not possible for many people who are self-employed or farming, about which I know something. You cannot reasonably expect them to forecast their incomes within close enough limits to serve the purposes of this bill, yet this is what they will be asked to do. Somebody must have drafted this bill. Did that person or the minister not realize it would not be possible for these people to forecast their incomes within reasonable limits?
I had been in this House for only a year and a half when the minister responsible for the post office adopted a policy of closing a number of rural post offices and a five-day work-week. I spent the better part of two years, off and on, fighting to keep open certain rural post offices in my constituency, which in my opinion, and the opinion of those people who lived there, were essential to the needs of the people. My batting average was about 25 per cent. For every one I persuaded the postmaster and those concerned at that time to keep open, probably two or three were closed. Now, the minister says this was a very bad mistake. The department should not have closed so many rural post offices, and should not have gone to a five-day week. He says some action will have to be taken to correct this mistake. Let me suggest to the government that the injustices it visited upon those people will not be corrected by this government. The injustices done to those people who received as little as $2,500 or $3,000 annually for running a post office in a community, and who were let out will not be corrected.
April 25, 1972

It is about time the government became aware of human factors, that it is not dealing with statistics but with flesh and blood people, who think, run, walk, sit and eat. They are not puppets that which, when the strings are pulled, bob up and down. It does not matter how many times you jerk the string of a puppet, it will bob up and down. However, if you are dealing with people and you jerk them around, it hurts. You might hurt them to the extent that the injury cannot easily be remedied. This might be the effect of the legislation now before the House.
Let me read you another part of this bill:
Where payment of a benefit is approved in respect of a benefit year, the benefit is payable for each month in that year commencing with the month following the month in which the application therefor is received, but if a benefit would have been payable before that month if an application therefor had been made, then the benefit is payable for each month commencing with the latter of
(a)	the 11th month preceding the month in which the application was received; and
(b)	the month in which a benefit would first have been payable if an application therefor had been made.
If hon. members were able to follow the sense of this bill, they must be pretty good. I have seen similar provisions in other bills proposed in respect of agricultural matters. As a result, we get programs like Lift. After these programs are in operation for a little while, we see a repetition of the post office scheme. A farmer or businessman operating a farm will say that the program is not working and ask that something be done about it. The government then begins to work its way through a tangle of bureaucracy to straighten out the program.
Let me say in all honesty to the minister that this is an unworkable proposition. I would be much better for Canadians if we continued to use the method we are now using. We should have universal payments which are tied to the cost of living in order that family allowances can keep pace with whatever degree of inflation occurs. If it is thought that this is a good method of supplementing income, two principles should be observed. Universality and the rate of inflation should be taken into account in respect of family allowances and old age pensions. The government should, when setting the tax rate, keep these principles in mind in order to take back the surplus at the upper end as well as look after the needs at the lower end.
I do not understand why there is such great concern to limit payments of this kind. The people who get them spend the money in any event. It goes into the stream. They are taxed on the money they receive. These payments are not like the dividends and earnings of corporations which go to Washington, London or Paris. This money stays in Canada and keeps working around through the stores, the service stations and the garment manufacturers. It goes the whole circle, and the tax collector, the wholesaler, retailer and the service station operator grab off their 5 per cent, 7 per cent or 10 per cent. This keeps the economy running. I think that instead of this miserly, penny-pinching attitude which has become so prevalent with this government in respect of our low income people, our senior citizens and so on, the government should adopt an attitude which would put some
Family Income Security Plan
purchasing power in the community. Perhaps then the government would not be plagued as it is now by the unemployment problem.
If the government would get the economy rolling so the people would have some purchasing power, we would not have the extremely high rate of unemployment we have now. One of the real problems is that we are getting fewer and fewer people with purchasing power and more and more people at the barest subsistence level which makes it necessary to pinch every penny. If someone could persuade the financial thinkers on the other side to turn their thoughts around a little bit and change their approach, then I believe perhaps we would do better. But, in closing, I suggest the only thing I can do is plead with the minister to withdraw this bill before he does irreparable harm to the total Canadian community.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to speak again on Bill C-170 by virtue of the NDP amendment. It has now been 17 months since the government revealed its intention to improve the family allowance system in Canada. For each month that passes $14.2 million is withheld from the poverty-stricken people of Canada. The delay has already been too long; to delay any longer would be intolerable. Poverty in Canada affects about a quarter of our population, and increased family allowance cheques will be of great value to them. Adjustment to the payment levels of family allowances has not been made since 1957 and is therefore long overdue. For these reasons, the Progressive Conservative members in the House of Commons will support the Liberal government's FISP bill at second reading.
This is not to say that we are satisfied with the bill as it stands. We are not. There are gross inequities, ambiguous clauses and costly provisions contained in Bill C-170 and our party is determined to make every effort to have Bill C-170 greatly improved during the committee stage.
In the first place, we dislike the fact that it is no longer stipulated in the legislation that family allowances are to be paid to the mother for the care and education of her children. The principle of Bill C-170 is not the principle of the Family Allowances Act, it is not the principle of the Youth Allowances Act and it is not the principle of the predecessor Bill C-264 of last session which was introduced in the House in September, 1971. Between that date and 15 March, 1972, when Bill C-170 was introduced, an entirely different principle, a totally different philosophy, a distinct legal concept, has been silently substituted.
The Family Allowances Act, the Youth Allowances Act and Bill C-264, all have one principle in common. That principle is that the benefits are established, paid and administered on the basis of a right that is vested in our children. The people of Canada, acting through their government, are the donors; the parents are the trustees, and the children have been and are the beneficiaries. Through Bill C-170, the government proposes to take away that right. Nowhere in his explanation of the bill on second reading did the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro) confess to the purpose of Bill C-170. Indeed, he implied that the rights of Canadian children, as established by parliament, will be maintained and even

Family Income Security Plan
enhanced. As can be seen from a reading of page 1133, first column, of Hansard for March 24,1972 he said:
FISP benefits will provide a basic income for each child upon which can be built additional supports as deemed appropriate by provincial or municipal authorities. We know that unemployment insurance does not make any special provision for children. Neither do old age security, the guaranteed income supplement, the Canada Pension Plan retirement pension or war veterans allowances.
He might have added that neither does FISP. Section 5 of the Family Allowances Act, as enacted by this parliament, provides that the allowance shall be applied by the person receiving it exclusively toward the maintenance, care, training, education and advancement of the child.
Section 5(1) of the Youth Allowances Act, as enacted by parliament provides:
An allowance payable to a parent in respect of a dependent youth shall be applied exclusively for the care, maintenance, education or advancement of such youth.
Clause 5(2) of Bill C-264, the Family Income Security Plan of last session provided:
That a benefit shall be applied:
a)	in the case of a child referred to in paragraph 3(1 Xa) exclusively toward the maintenance, care, training, education or advancement of the child in respect of whom it was paid, and
b)	in the case of a person referred to in paragraph 3(l)b) exclusively toward the maintenance, care, training, education or advancement of the person in respect of whom it was paid in such manner as prescribed by the regulations.
Those trust provisions for the benefit of the children of Canada do not appear in Bill C-170. Instead, that bill takes away the vested right of the children, a right which the minister said was the only right they possessed. And what does Bill C-170 propose to substitute? It proposes outright grants to adults. The children become part of a formula upon which the right of the adult is based and calculated. I hope the minister might be able to clarify this.
Clause 5 provides that the recipient of the allowance shall be the parent or other authorized person. The definitions of "family" and "parent" mention the child as being in the custody and control of such person. Clause 3(1), page 3 and Clause 4(3)(a) and (b) on page 4 mention that such person must be wholly or substantially maintained by such person. No mention is made of the fact that the child must be cared for, trained, educated or advanced. The child is merely a hook upon which to hang a grant.
Another weakness in the bill, Mr. Speaker, is the cut-off levels. There is certainly an obvious inconsistency among government departments in their assessment of when families need government support. The Minister of National Health and Welfare takes into account the fact that it costs more to raise a child once he reaches the age of 12 years, whereas the Minister of Finance in his new Income Tax Act, did not recognize that children are more expensive until they reach age 16. Similarly, the Minister of National Health and Welfare believes that any family with one child and a gross income of $4,500. or less should get maximum assistance from his department, yet the recycled Minister of Finance continues to impose a substantial tax on the same person.
In fact, there is a wide range of problems associated with Bill C-170's treatment of cut-off levels. Family income security penalizes working wives, particularly in

the lower and middle income classes, through its cut-off levels being based on gross family income. If a wife goes out to work to supplement her husband's meagre salary, it is quite likely that her added income will push total family income above the cut-off level, and she will therefore forfeit part or all of her family allowance cheques as a result. For a family struggling to make ends meet, the loss of a baby bonus cheque hurts. Consequently, FISP has a built-in provision which discourages working mothers because they know they will probably lose part or all of their family allowance cheque as a result.
The importance of this to middle income earners cannot be underestimated. A March 23, 1972 publication by Statistics Canada on the indebtedness of Canadians showed that in the income group from $7,000 to $10,000 per year, only 37 per cent had no debt, and the average debt of debtors was a whopping $1,668. Cut-off levels should be based on net income after deductions rather than on gross income. In this way, personal income tax exemptions and child care deductions will have their full effect for working wives. Benefit cut-off levels can then still be scaled to ensure that poverty stricken families benefit most from family allowances.
Because of the provision that family allowance payments made under the authority of this piece of legislation are based on gross rather than net income with no automatic cost of living escalator, more and more lower and middle class Canadians will find themselves progressively cut off from family allowance payments over the years as their incomes rise, even though inflation may increase proportionately. Although Bill C-170, unlike its predecessor Bill C-264, has a clause providing for an increase in benefit levels and payments because of cost of living increases, the procedure involved is not automatic but is left to the whim of the Minister of National Health and Welfare, who is responsible for proposing the increase to the cabinet. Then, at the whim of the cabinet, the proposal may or may not be accepted. It is subject also to delays in the House of Commons, where a resolution is necessary to approve the order of the Governor in Council. The lack of an automatic cost of living escalator clause in FISP means that neither benefit levels nor benefit payments are scaled to take into account the erosion effect that inflation will have in the future.
Since 1961, personal income per capita has almost doubled, rising from $1,613 to $3,092. This does not mean that many fewer people are living in poverty as inflation has considerably eroded the relative buying power of the dollar in the interim. While personal incomes are rising, though, cut-off lines for both maximum and partial FISP benefit payments are stationary. Consequently, if personal incomes double again over the next ten years, for example, more and more people would find themselves disqualified to FISP payments because their incomes had risen above the stationary cut-off lines. Yet, many of these disqualified people may still be defined by Statistics Canada as living near the poverty line.
There should, therefore, be an automatic cost of living escalator clause, not just a discretionary cost of living escalator clause as there is in Bill C-170. Use or non-use of this clause can be subject to political abuse. This escalator
April 25, 1972

provision in Bill C-170 is out of step with other federal legislation, such as the Canada Pension Plan and the Old Age Security Act which guarantee some, even if too little, increases each year in line with cost of living increases. Therefore, it is wise to insist now before the FISP bill is first enacted, that benefit levels be automatically subject each year to a cost of living increase commensurate with the rise in the consumer price index.
With regard to the gross income levels provision in Bill C-170, I ask the minister to clarify the criteria for establishing the gross or net income for the farmer, the fisherman, the sawmill operator or the independent trucker. If their family allowance payments are based on their gross income, then the government is being grossly unfair since these people have necessary capital expenditures to maintain the equipment essential for their livelihood.
In addition to all these problems connected with the gross income provisions in Bill C-170, there is another glaring weakness which has been noted more than once by many speakers. I refer to the administrative load that will occur as a result of some sections of the bill. Changes in income of families who work seasonally are going to cause utter confusion, since they are required to submit periodically increases or decreases in their earnings. Let us take for example the family with one child earning $4,500 a year and receiving the maximum benefit. The wife might go to work and earn enough in a few months to put the family beyond that income ceiling. According to the experts, even if the combined family income reaches beyond that level, the family will continue to draw the maximum benefit for that year. However, if their income is above that ceiling again the next year, even though they continue to draw the maximum benefits, they will have to repay 33 cents for every $100 they earned over the basic income ceiling in the previous year.
It has been estimated by the Department of National Health and Welfare that administrative costs during the first year of FISP's operation will rise to about $13.5 million, and when FISP is fully operational, it is likely that administrative costs will escalate very rapidly. The Liberal government anticipates that when FISP has been fully implemented, the staff involved in processing FISP will number 1,477, more than twice the current staff of 730. Undoubtedly, this will push annual administrative costs much higher in the future.
There are many who argue, quite justifiably, that the combined administrative costs of many income security programs represent a sizeable total sum, and that this sum would be more effective given directly into the hands of the poor. According to this argument, the consolidation and rationalization of our welfare structures could significantly reduce the costs currently involved in administering a profusion of welfare programs. The money recouped from such a streamlining of the welfare structure could then provide additional money for actual welfare work. An income security scheme administered entirely through the income tax structure would accomplish this end by decreasing the number of administrative bureaucracies for welfare now scattered through several federal departments. The question is: can we therefore justify the increased administrative costs of Bill C-170
Family Income Security Plan
over the present plan, when such costs may be unnecessary?
A further problem connected with the present bill concerns the provision that children in institutions across the country will receive only half of the maximum FISP benefit payments. This is contrary both to the old family allowance plan, Bill C-264, and the Quebec provincial family allowance scheme announced in 1971. Just today, the hon. member for Moncton (Mr. Thomas) passed me a telegram which came from the Hon. Mrs. Brenda Robertson, minister of welfare for New Brunswick. This telegram is worth reading in full. It reads:
In reviewing Bill C-170 as proposed by the government of Canada it has been noted that subsection 2 of section 6 makes provision to restrict by 50 per cent the amount of FISP benefits payable to children whose maintenance costs are shared under the Canada Assistance Plan. My government expresses strong opposition to this provision and urgently requests that it be reconsidered. If FISP were to be paid solely on the basis of family size with the payments of benefits commencing with the third or fourth child, then it might be logical to state that children who are the responsibility of government departments are not affected. However, this is not the basis of FISP benefits. The concept that FISP is income related and therefore provincial governments require less financial assistance to maintain children in care is hardly valid in relation to the Atlantic provinces. The current provision in Bill C-170 will mean that children who are in care will receive virtually no increase in the amount of money available for their maintenance while children in their own homes will be significantly better off. I believe this is very unfair. My government urges you to reconsider the implications of subsection 2 of section 6 of Bill C-170. As it stands it is discriminatory to a large number of children.
Another fault with Bill C-170 as it is presently constituted-and I will end my recital of the bill's errors here, although I could continue indefinitely-concerns the Trudeau government's failure to include a date on which the new scheme would become effective and benefits be paid. The government's family income security bill of last session, C-264, was to come into effect this May 1, a date a few days away. That provision has been removed. The government has adopted instead a drafting gimmick to delude the public. Clause 2(1) defines benefit year as "any period after August 1972, consisting of twelve consecutive months commencing with the first day of September". How many families awaiting these increased benefits promised under the bill have assumed they will get them as of September 1, 1972? In fact, that provision means only that no benefits can be paid before that date. Again, Bill C-170 will become effective on Royal Assent. This is only another gimmick to give the appearance of action by the government to pay out benefits as quickly as possible, presumably in September of this year.
Although this bill will become law on Royal Assent, that assent will be subject to section 3(4) which provides that no benefit is payable under the act for any month in a benefit year for which an allowance is payable under the Family Allowances Act. Section 24 will provide that the Family Allowances Act will only be repealed at the discretion of the government. When will that discretion be exercised? The Minister of National Welfare has remained mum on this aspect. Is he afraid that this measure will join the Hazardous Products Act and other acts, of which only parts were put into effect?

Family Income Security Plan
I have elaborated at length on the faults of Bill C-170, Mr. Speaker, for a very important reason. That reason is that the Progressive Conservatives consider the bill to be loose and sloppy in its conception and in its drafting. Although we have agreed to support the bill on second reading, for reasons on which I have already elaborated, we make no commitment to support any further stage of the bill unless substantial changes correcting these faults are agreed to by the government. We reserve the right on third reading to take action as we see fit, depending on how the bill comes out of committee.
One of the ways in which the inadequacies and faults of the family allowance plan of Bill C-170 could be rectified is through the formula offered in the amendment proposed by the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis). Our party is supporting the principle of the NDP amendment because it is an umbrella under which substantial improvements can be made such as increased payments, a better break for middle income earners, less administrative costs, etc. However, we believe that the drafting of the amendment is quite as loose as the drafting of the bill. We can assure the House that our amendments on the family allowance plan, to be submitted in committee, will improve the bill and not be merely vague, meaningless phrases.
The reasoned amendment put forward by the leader of the NDP is so general and broad in scope as to encompass any scheme of increased family allowances, provided only that the principle of universality of payment is retained. I say "universality of payment" because the "universality of benefit" is in doubt. It is quite possible to grant "substantial" payments under the scheme and yet tax every cent of those benefits away by making related changes, as the amendment calls for, in the Income Tax Act. On the other hand, it is equally possible, within the terms of the amendment, to establish a plan of family benefits that is far preferable to the government plan proposed in Bill C-170. It is for that reason we propose to vote for this amendment. In spite of our agreement to support this amendment, however, we do not support many of the ill-advised statements that the hon. member for York South made in introducing the amendment to the House.
The first thing that I have to take issue with, and that I find difficult to understand, is why he should deliberately alarm the low income and "no income" earners of the country. He intimated that his reading of the act is the only way in which it can be read, when he stated very emphatically that all citizens of this country who are receiving social assistance will only receive half the benefits provided under this bill.
He used these exact words, Mr. Speaker, and I quote from page 1445 of Hansard:
What the bill says is that not only children in institutions will get half the benefit but that children of all families on social welfare will get only half the benefit.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker, and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). Many of the clauses referred to by the hon. member for York South are ambiguous, I agree, and even ridiculous. This fact was pointed out very clearly by George Bain of the Globe and Mail in one of his columns. But it is irresponsible for the member for York South, merely for the sake of political advantage, to read these clauses as he wants to read them and, again I say, to deliberately alarm the people of Canada who have been waiting for years to derive some benefits promised to them. Why not take his grievance out on the supposed legal advisers who concocted the bill, those supposed experts who sit and try to make things as complicated as possible, but do not know the meaning of the words, "human being" or "poverty"?
The Minister of National Health and Welfare tried to rise in his place last Wednesday and put the record straight. Instead of allowing him to do so, the rules of this institution prevented him, so that the words of confusion could go out to the poverty stricken of this country who wonder now just how much benefit they will get under this bill. The minister, who was listening, made mention that this provision applied only to the children in institutions. This interpretation is confirmed by members of the Department of National Health and Welfare, who indicate that only children who are in the complete care of the parent would lose half the benefit under the present provisions of the bill-I should say who are not in the complete care of the parent.
In another part of his speech, the Leader of the New Democratic Party wondered aloud whether members of the House, and especially those from Newfoundland and Quebec, had even read the bill. Well, Mr. Speaker, I am one of those members, and I can assure him that I have read the bill. And I can tell him that I have read the white paper on income security that was issued back in 1970 containing the government's ideas on family income security and the promises to the poverty stricken in Canada. I read Bill C-264, too, when the government introduced that bill which promised low income families that they would receive increases by May 1, 1972. I read the Throne Speeches since 1968, when I first came here, promising equality of opportunity, and indicating what the government owed to the poverty stricken of this country. I have read and watched and listened, with frustration and
April 25, 1972

confusion to the deliberate political strategy that this government has been using since 1970, using the poverty stricken families of our nation for political advantage and building up their hopes falsely with utter and contemptible disregard for human beings. I do not need anybody to tell me what I have read or missed.
I read thousands of letters from my constituents who sent me here to represent them, letters telling me they do not have enough money to feed their children and have to send them to bed cold and hungry, letters from mothers asking me to help them because they have to go to court for failure to pay their school fees and have to deny their children the right to an education. I read more hundreds of letters from mothers telling me that they cannot send their children to school because they cannot afford to buy them clothing. I read more hundreds and thousands of letters from mothers and fathers asking me for help from the government to buy them enough materials to fix holes in the roofs of their homes, or for bedding or for a stove to heat their homes, because they cannot afford to give these necessities to their children.
Here is one letter from a doctor who says that a certain constituent of mine is mentally defective, is an epileptic and is also suffering with nerves, anxiety and tension while living in a house which is unfit for human habitation. That was on August 10, 1971 and now, almost a year later, the husband writes to me and asks how he is to get a better home for his wife and children when he cannot get anybody to answer his letters.
I read these letters coming into my office at the rate of a couple of hundred a week. I answer each and every one of them myself because I am concerned. I tell them to have a little hope because I want to have a little faith that perhaps the government still has some humane consideration for our children. But after four years I, like these many thousands of mothers of children, am becoming more and more frustrated at the lack of sincerity which exists here. Yes, Mr. Speaker, the words come out from the Trudeau government and everybody else. They flow like water- the millions of words, and the hundreds of bogus promises-but that is where it ends.
I read everything, Mr. Speaker, everything that I can in the time allotted to me. I hope when the minister has the opportunity to speak he will clarify the serious inequities in the bill so that with sincerity we can consult and put the bill in proper order at the committee stage for the greatest benefit of all Canadians.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, members of the New Democratic Party are going to vote against passage of this bill at second reading stage, are going to oppose this bill in committee and I presume, unless the government changes its basic philosophy, will vote against this bill on third reading. The reasons are simple. We shall vote against this bill because not only is it wrong in principle but it reverses and wipes out a basic concept established in this country, not by a radical socialist government but by a Liberal government led by Mackenzie King.
Family Income Security Plan
The Family Allowances Act, when first introduced, provided for the payment of family allowances to all families with children entitled to receive benefits, regardless of income. Speaking in connection with suggestions that the old age pension should only be paid to those in need, another former Liberal prime minister, Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent, made it clear that he believed in universal old age pensions and that he believed those few old age pensioners with incomes so high they did not really need the old age pension would be relieved of their surplus income by the income tax. We may be old fashioned; however, I suggest to the Liberal Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro) that we are not so radical when we continue to stand for the principle of universality, a principle which was not first proposed by a Liberal government but which was first implemented by a Liberal government in connection with the Family Allowances Act and the old age pension.
Under the provisions of this bill, payments will be made on a selective basis. The universal principle contained in the Family Allowances Act and the old age pension legislation will be, as I have already mentioned, wiped out. This, I suggest, is not only a regressive step; it is an unjustifiable step. The payment of benefits will be based on a sliding and complex formula which will make the major difficulties recently experienced by people unfortunate enough to be unemployed seem trivial. I am talking of the difficulties of those people who have had to file claims for unemployment insurance benefits. Their claims have been pushed from pillar to post. They have had to wait six, eight, ten and even 15 weeks for their claims to be processed, the reasons for delay being that the computer broke down, that the people in the Unemployment Insurance Commission did not understand the provisions of the act, and so on. Many reasons, it is alleged, were behind these difficulties. I am certain that the situation in Winnipeg not only can be duplicated, but has been and is being duplicated every day of the week in the home city of the Minister of National Health and Welfare. I say that the difficulties experienced by those who could not obtain their unemployment insurance benefits will seem simple and trivial compared with the difficulties which will occur after this bill becomes law.
It has been estimated that the effects of this bill will divide people and neighbours, group by group. Let me attempt to give some concrete illustrations to show how this bill will operate and have that effect. First, 25 per cent of Canadian families will be better off. We have never questioned that. Those who will be better off certainly need the extra assistance they will get under this bill. However, over 40 per cent of all families will receive only partial benefits, and half of this group will get less money than they are getting now. One third of all families will be cut off from all benefits.
I said, when I began, that we oppose this movement away from the principle of universality. We think that principle is a sound one. That principle found favour with the overwhelming proportion of the Canadian people and there is no reason, aside from political reasons which I will speak about later, for the government to wipe out in this legislation the basic principle of universality. As I

April 25, 1972
Family Income Security Plan
said before, let us consider some concrete illustrations. Let us see how this bill will work.
The family with an income of $5,001 per year and one child will not receive any baby bonus at all. Does the Minister of National Health and Welfare really believe that a family of three with an income of just over $5,000 has an income so large that it does not need the family allowance? The family with two children under ten years with an income of $9,001 will be cut off. There are many people in Hamilton, many workers in the steel works and other plants, who now earn $9,000 a year. That is the family income, particularly if the wife is working part time. Considering today's cost of living, the cost of food, which is rising every month, the cost of fuel for heating homes, which is rising regularly, and taxes, which are constantly going up, does the minister really believe that a family of four in this country with an income of $9,000 is doing so well that it does not need even the level of assistance being given to it by the family allowances plan at present?
Let us consider the family with five children under 12 years of age with a total income of $11,001 per year. There you have a family of seven, Mr. Speaker, and it will not receive any family allowance under the new act. An income of $11,000 may sound like a pretty fair income. Does the minister think that a family of seven living in Toronto, Montreal, Winnipeg, Vancouver or Hamilton does not need the assistance it is getting under the Family Allowances Act at present? If he thinks that he has moved a long way from the people he represents since coming to Ottawa in 1962.
My party has always supported the principle of universality in programs of social security. I ask, why has the government party, which introduced in legislative form universal programs, abandoned the principle of universality which it first introduced? The reason is not that it does not believe in universality. The reason is that the government intends to phase out the program of family allowances altogether, because it does not think that program is a successful tool for fighting poverty. The family allowances program, Mr. Speaker, was never introduced for the purpose of fighting poverty. The payments were never considered, by the government which introduced them, by the opposition parties or by the general public, as welfare payments. And they were not welfare payments. If the government wants to help the poor people of this country, goodness knows, there is much that it can do and that needs to be done.
I put some figures on record yesterday which show that the bottom 40 per cent of income earners in this country get just under 16 per cent of the total incomes earned in this country. There is no question about the bottom one third of the population needing assistance. If the government wants to mount a war on poverty, there are much more effective ways of doing it than taking away the family allowance from people in the lower income group. That is what this bill does.
Why does the government not stop the massive giveaways which in the past few years have amounted to hundreds of millions of dollars as the result of programs

of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion which supposedly foster the establishment of industries in slow growth areas. Grants have been made of hundreds of millions of dollars. To whom have they been made? They have been made to the most affluent, largest corporations in this country, most of them multi-national corporations in the United States. If the government really wants to fight poverty, why does it not wipe out these give-aways and give the money to those who need it?
If the government wants to fight poverty, it should do something about plugging the loopholes in our tax system. I am not going to repeat the arguments put so well by the hon. member for Duvernay (Mr. Kierans), but the facts are as he put them in his famous speech to the Canadian Economic Association. Some of the largest corporations in this country, oil companies such as Imperial Oil and Shell Oil and mining companies such as international Nickel and Noranda, to mention just a few, are legally evading paying the major share of the taxes which they ought to be paying. I do not even want to compare the taxes they pay with what individuals pay, but if they paid their fair share of taxes as other corporations do, they would pay approximately a 50 per cent corporation tax. In fact, they are paying taxes on probably 10 per cent or less of their earnings. Why? Because this government has continued the policy under which this country has suffered for many years by giving special tax concessions to oil and mining companies as well as others.
If the government wants to do something to combat poverty and help the people who are in real need, it should not take away the family allowance from the middle income bracket. It should take money from those who have it. This government will not do that because it is dependent on the 95 largest corporations in this country for the major share of the campaign expenses of the Liberal party at the time of elections. That is why this government will not take that very sensible and equitable step.
This proposal of the government will take away benefits which the moderate income group has had since 1944 and give increased benefits to those who are really poor. We have stated many times that we will support every proposal to increase the economic wellbeing of people in the lower income bracket. However, that should not be done at the expense of those working people in the middle-class group.
The government's proposals will divide the people in this country. Some will not receive anything under the new FISP program. Some will receive less that at present and others will receive more. Neighbors with relatively similar incomes and circumstances will be treated in different ways. I cannot think of a better way to divide the citizens of this country than the plan devised by the minister-I was going to say the minister and his department.
