speechtext:
I have too much respect for the ability and social vision of the officials of the minister's department to believe they had anything to do with the formulation of this bill. I think this bill was drafted by the politicians to meet their political ends. If the minister had the courage to table and publish the white paper prepared by his
April 25, 1972

deputy minister, the charge I have just made would be proven conclusively.
Implementation of this bill will create an administrative jungle. The minister estimated that the number of employees required to process FISP cheques will more than double. I am certain that is a gross under-estimate of what will actually happen. Costs of other departments will be as great if not greater than the direct cost the minister outlined when he introduced this bill. The Tax Appeal Board, the Department of National Revenue, the Department of Supply and Services and the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development will need extra staff. The Department of Manpower and Immigration will be affected. Statistics Canada will also be involved in this. All this will cost money and will create bottlenecks which will mean that people will have to wait for their cheques.
What about the potential recipients of the benefits under this plan? They will have to provide the department with the necessary information, and that is not going to be easy. Every time there is an increase in income, a layoff or a change in the age of a child, the potential benefit will be changed. All this will have to be understood and calculated by the people involved. After the information is gathered, the paperwork must still be done.
Let us look at how this bill operates. As an example, I will refer to a steelworker in Hamilton whom the Minister of National Health and Welfare represents. It is not unusual that in negotiations at the end of a contract a steelworker, a member of a building trade union or of any other organized group in Hamilton, will receive a 25 cent an hour increase in their wage rate. According to my calculations, and I think my arithmetic is correct, an increase of 25 cents an hour in terms of a 40 hour work week in a 52 week year means an increased annual income of just over $500. So, Mr. Speaker, if a worker obtains an increase of just over $500 a year, his income category is changed and he has to recalculate the amount to which he is entitled under the new plan. He has to fill in a new form; it has to be processed and checked. If the wife of a steelworker works full time and earns more than $500, that too, changes the category. If a steelworker is laid off for three or four weeks he will lose more than $500 in pay. He will then be entitled to more money under the plan. Every time there is a change in family income, new calculations will be required and new forms will have to be completed. How can the ordinary citizen be expected to handle all this? Even on the unlikely assumption that citizens follow all these instructions correctly, the work of administering these constantly changing records will create a chaotic jungle.
I am sure no member of parliament who represents ordinary working people can stay long in his office without receiving calls or letters from constituents who are encountering difficulties in connection with the Unemployment Insurance Act since the recent changes came into effect. I am not complaining about these calls; I regard attending to them as part of the job of a member of parliament. But the number of calls members of parliament are expected to deal with in connection with unemployment insurance will amount to a minute trickle com-
Family Income Security Plan
pared with the enquiries which every member will receive should this new plan become operative.
There is no need, Mr. Speaker, for this administrative jungle to develop, except perhaps, a political need. And what is the political need? It is not difficult to explain. The government understands quite well that people in the lower income brackets are no longer able to manage on the incomes they are receiving, because of the increased cost of living and other factors. It realizes that substantial improvements are needed in the incomes of these people. However, as I indicated earlier, the government is not prepared to get the money necessary to increase the incomes of those in the lower income bracket from those who have it, from those in the higher income brackets and from the corporations which are not paying their fair share of taxes. So, the government is proposing to take money which has been given to people who are, really, poor people in that lower and middle income brackets, and redistribute it to people who are desperately poor. We reject an approach of that kind.
I want to be fair to the government. I do not intend to do what a number of my hon. friends have done by outlining in detail once again what our party thinks should be done. I know the minister would say, with some justification, that I was being partisan. I am partisan, but I try to be fair. I suggest to the minister that he look again, if he has not done so already, at the policy statement issued by the Canadian Council on Social Development in April, 1971. This Council is not a wide-eyed radical organization. It is not an organization whose purpose is to destroy this country and rebuild it on an entirely new set of principles. It is a council of organizations which deals with, and occasionally represents, people who need assistance. Its policy statement amounts to a fundamental rejection of the proposals which the minister is making in this bill.
Let me take just a few minutes in which to put on record what the Canadian Council on Social Development says.
The Council fully endorses the family allowance goals of help to all families with dependent children, and a greater measure of equality of opportunity for all children, i.e., special emphasis on the needs of low income families. However, it believes that it is needlessly costly and cumbersome to attempt to include these aims and a meaningful attack on poverty for all people in one income maintenance measure, as appears to be the ultimate goal for FISP.
In relation to the attack on poverty, a comprehensive and integrated income security program is required which takes account of the costs of child-rearing.
The Council believes that the feasible and desirable approach to a reformed family allowances program is a general family allowance plan that takes care of a substantial proportion of child-rearing costs. The net benefits should be related more closely than now to other income resources, and the balance of the child-rearing costs should be completely covered for low-income people through a separate but integrated guaranteed income program as part of a comprehensive approach to income security.
Let me point out that the Council rejects the government's proposal to cease paying family allowances to all families with dependent children, and that it calls on the government to inaugurate a guaranteed income program. Dealing with the basic elements of any family allowances program, the Council enunciates the following guiding principles. I will quote again:
The Council believes that:
1616

April 25, 1972
Family Income Security Plan
(a)	Family allowances should be universal, paid to all families
with dependent children as a social right thus avoiding divisiveness among families and any element of stigma. The present
program has this feature but FISP would eliminate it.
When I was talking earlier about the divisiveness of this program, the minister suggested, in an interjection which was probably not recorded in Hansard, that my speech would promote division. I would point out that the Canadian Council on Social Development agrees with what I said, and I agree with them that the minister's program will divide the people of Canada. The Council goes on to say:
There should be equity in relation to family responsibilities and to the financial and other resources of families. Three criteria cited by the federal white paper, Income Security for Canadians, are size of family, age of children, and family income. Of these, the present program only takes age into account and FISP only considers income.
There should be the maximum feasible simplicity and efficiency in administration. These features are virtues of the present family allowances program but FISP would undoubtedly be considerably more complicated and costly to administer.
The program should be as fully compatible as possible with long-term social and fiscal policies. This is not evident in the FISP proposals.
The program should have a burlt-in escalation clause to meet the full amount of annual rises in the cost of living. This feature is not included in either the present program or FISP.
There should be integration of all programs of allowances for dependent children, i.e., youth allowances should be integrated with family allowances as proposed ill FISP.
There is the analysis of the minister's proposals made by what I think is a most representative and knowledgeable organization, one with a membership encompassing the vast majority, if not all, of those organizations in Canada, both government and vol intary, that have as their task helping people in need. It is obvious from the short summary that I have put on the record that the Canadian Council on Social Development has the gravest reservations regarding these proposals. When I say that, I am being very cautious and conservative in my estimate of what they say. I really believe they are rejecting out of hand the basic principles on which the minister has based his FISP proposals.
I urge the minister to take the time to consider these basic objections to his proposals by the Canadian Council on Social Development. These are objections made by an organization which cannot, by the wildest stretch of the imagination, be termed a partisan organization, one with any political axe to grind. It has no objective other than to help the people of this country who are in need. The minister may believe that the Canadian Council on Social Development is wrong in its analysis. If so, he ought to take the time at an early date to explain in what way the objections raised to his plan by this very important organization are unacceptable to him.
The minister may believe that the implementation of a program such as that proposed by the Canadian Council on Social Development is financially impracticable. This is the usual reason given for rejecting proposals made by members of the New Democratic Party. In this respect, I would point out that the members of the board of the Canadian Council on Social Development are, in the

main, pretty responsible businessmen and civil servants at the federal, provincial or municipal level. There are also one or two representatives from the labour movement, and there may be one or two representatives from what is now commonly known as poor people's organizations. But the overwhelming majority of the members of the board and committees of this organization are responsible, knowledgeable, well informed citizens. If the government is rejecting their proposals and criticisms of its plan because it believes that the country could not afford to adopt them at this time, then the minister ought to say so.
I suggest that the criticisms and suggestions made by this organization ought not to be dismissed as summarily as they have been dismissed by the minister and the government. As I said earlier, in face of what I consider to be the virtually unanimous rejection of the proposals in this bill by those organizations best able to assess the needs of the people that we hope to help through this type of legislation, I can see no reason why the members of this party, indeed why any member of this parliament, should vote for the bill on second reading, at committee stage, or on third reading. Like the other members of this party I intend to oppose this bill.

speechtext:
that Bill C-13, to amend the Combines Investigation Act (floor penalties, criminal joint tortfeasors, and moieties), be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I have proposed this bill in view of my long held conviction that the laws of this country ought to apply with some degree of equality to all citizens of this country.
It is not uncommon in this country on any day of the week for one to pick up a newspaper, whether it be in Ottawa, Toronto, Montreal, Winnipeg or Vancouver, and read about a person who appeared in a magistrate's court charged with the theft of an article worth a relatively small amount from a store or supermarket. If it is a first offence, the person in question may be let off with a reprimand or a fine. But we can be certain that if it is a second or a third offence, the person so charged will get a jail sentence. It is usual to find in the jails and prisons of Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and also in northwestern Ontario that a large percentage, 50 per cent or more, of the inmates are of Indian or Metis origin. Many of them were convicted of some offence which was committed as a result of excessive drinking. Many of them are in jail because they could not pay the fine which the magistrate or judge imposed as an alternative to the jail term.
Recently, in the province of Quebec, there was a strike by Public Service employees. It is certainly not for me to discuss here this afternoon the reasons or justifications for that strike. Suffice to say, for the purpose of my discussions today, that a dozen or more of the people involved in that strike, who did not heed an injunction order that the strike be terminated, were sentenced by a judge to six months in prison. I do not know about other members of this Chamber, but I was struck by the pictures I saw in various newspapers of a group of young women in their twenties being carted off to jail for six months because of their involvement in the strike. I am not going to discuss this afternoon what I consider to be too severe sentences, but I give these illustrations in order to compare this kind of sentence on the part of Canadian judges with the kind of sentences handed out to some of the most prominent and highly respected corporations of this country after convictions under the combines act.
We have had this kind of legislation on our statute books in Canada for more than 50 years, during which time there have been perhaps more than 100 prosecutions and convictions, with something in the neighbourhood of hundreds of thousands of dollars paid in fines following the conviction of the offending corporations. In many cases, in spite of the conviction, and in spite of the fact that a number of the largest corporations in this country have been found guilty not just once but more than once
Combines Investigation Act
and ordered to cease and desist, the courts have never in any of these cases imposed a penalty other than a fine.
The purpose of my bill is to strengthen the penalties for crime committed in violation of the combines and monopolies act. It will amend a present section of the act which contains no floor for the penalty. The bill does not interfere with the penalty for a first offence, but provides that on a second offence there shall be a mandatory minimum jail term of one year and, on conviction of a third or subsequent offence, a mandatory minimum jail term of two years. The maximum jail term remains at two years.
Before spending a few minutes discussing the history of one of two of these cases, let me refer to a case which was reported in the Toronto Globe and Mail last Saturday, April 23, 1972. The headline reads "Ready-mix firms fined $245,000". Let me quote a few paragraphs of the story as follows:
Twelve firms that admitted conspiring to prevent or lessen unduly competition in the production, manufacture, sale or supply of ready-mixed concrete between 1961 and 1968 were fined a total of $245,000 by Mr. Justice John Osier yesterday.
In total, the fine is the largest so far imposed in Ontario for breach of the Combines Investigation Act-considering the number of firms involved and the fact that all are first offenders. Heavier fines have been imposed in the past on other corporations, but they involved companies that operate in more than one province or across Canada.
Later on, the story reads, in part:
Mr. Justice Osier said the offences were committed over 7i years, and that not all the firms were in existence for that time or had participated in the combination for the whole period. The firms advertised themselves as suppliers of ready-mixed concrete in the Metro area.
Representatives of the offending firms met often and discussed prices, Mr. Justice Osier said.
A fine of $245,000 sounds like a lot of money, but when members compare this kind of offence and penalty with offences and penalties in respect of someone who steals $10 worth of groceries or a $50 suit, they must ask themselves how much the people of Metro Toronto overpaid because of the illegal combination by these companies to keep up prices.
It has been estimated by one magazine article recently that the over-payment in the Metropolitan Toronto area by those who have built homes, by municipalities which built roads and by the province which built highways, amounted to something in the neighbourhood of $30 million. I suggest to hon. members that the payment of $245,000 in fines is a pretty small price to pay in comparison with the illegal profits in the neighbourhood of $30 million. That is why I think legislation outlining and regulating combines needs to be strengthened.
Let me put on the record in the few minutes I have left at my disposal some illustrations of companies which have been guilty of violating our laws dealing with combines more than once. In 1960, the Abitibi Power and Paper Company was fined $15,000 for an offence under this legislation. The company's net profit in 1962 was $15.5 million; $13.7 million in 1961 and over $12 million in 1960.1 ask again, of what importance is a $15,000 fine to a company which has the kind of profits I have outlined? The St. Lawrence Corporation was fined $3,000 in 1958 and
1618

Combines Investigation Act
$20,000 in 1960. Its profits in 1959 were over $6 million; in 1960, over $7 million and in 1961 they were over $7 million again. The Goodyear Tire and Rubber Company was convicted twice in 1953 and paid a fine of $10,000 on the occasion of each conviction. In 1959, that company made a profit of $2.3 million; in 1960, a profit of $2.9 million, and in 1961 a profit of over $3.5 million.
I could go on with innumerable similar illustrations. However, let me speak for a moment about the kind of people who are involved in these transactions, because after all corporations are not operated by some kind of faceless individuals. They have offices and directors. Let us see who some of these people are. Bathurst Power and Paper Company has been convicted of violating the anticombines laws. Then, we have the St. Lawrence Corporation which was convicted in 1959. Who were some of its directors? One was Mr. R. H. Winters.

I think it is. It is very important for the people of this country to compare how ordinary citizens are dealt with when they appear in the courts. I suggest to the hon. member for York East (Mr. Otto), if he has not done so, that he should take a look at the reports of how two citizens in metropolitan Toronto were dealt with recently as reported in the Toronto Globe and Mail and compare their harsh, brusque, insensitive, discourteous treatment by the Justice of the Peace or the judge who dealt with them with the kind of treatment meted out to the officers of corporations such as those to which I have referred. This is precisely the point I am making and the reason I have raised this matter.
The St. Lawrence Corporation which was convicted in 1959 had on its board Mr. McCutcheon, Mr. E. P. Taylor and a host of others. Members will say quite justifiably that writing into the legislation a provision which would make mandatory a jail sentence on the occasion of a second or third offence will not stop illegal combinations. Certainly, members on the government side will say that the new competition act will deal much more effectively with illegal combinations in the future than the combines legislation has up until now. Well, the people of this country have lived for 50 years with anti-combines legislation brought forward by Liberal governments. We have seen the largest corporations of this country ignore the law. We have seen them combine to break the law to illegally maintain prices at an exorbitant height. We have seen governments, both Liberal and Conservative, do virtually nothing about the constant and repeated breaking of a law which is just as important to the people of this country as the laws under which poor people in the cities and Indians in the villages and reservations are sent to jail.
I do not believe the enactment of the provision I propose will make the corporations suddenly live up to the law, but I think it would go some distance towards making the ordinary citizens of this country believe that the law treats the rich in the same way it treats the poor, which in my opinion it does not do at the present time.

Mr. Speaker, a bill in

identical terms has been introduced by the hon. member at nearly every session of Parliament since 1963. It has been debated three times, namely, June 5,1964; November 4, 1966, and March 15, 1968. The references to sections of the Combines Investigation Act in this bill are to those in the act as found in R.S.C. 1970, Chapter C-23, which came into force on July 15, 1971.
The principal part of the bill, sections 1 to 6, is taken up with providing for mandatory minimum terms of imprisonment of one year and two years for second and third breaches respectively of prohibition orders, and for second and third offences respectively against the provisions relating to conspiracy in restraint of trade, merger, monopoly, discriminatory and predatory pricing, discriminatory promotional allowances and resale price maintenance. A court may now impose a sentence of up to two years' imprisonment for a first offence. By virtue of section 646 of the Criminal Code, however, a fine in the discretion of the court may be imposed in addition to or in lieu of imprisonment. The intent of the provisions of the bill, however, is that on conviction for a second or third offence the Court would be required to impose a sentence of imprisonment.
The proposed changes would not affect corporations which, of course, cannot be imprisoned, and under section 647 of the Criminal Code a fine in the discretion of the court may be imposed. To some extent, the proposed amendments are impractical in that corporate officials or employees are not necessarily in one position for too long, so that officials or employees concerned in a second offence could quite likely be different from those convicted in the first instance. The proposed amendments might, therefore, have little practical effect. Also, if the offence concerns a different product line, for example, paperboard, pulpwood, containerboard or fine paper as in the paper industry, the courts do not always appear to have considered an offence, involving a different product line from that in respect of which the firms were first convicted, as a second offence.
Actually, what is intended to be raised by this bill is the perennial question of whether corporate officers, officials or employees should be prosecuted in addition to, or in lieu of, the corporation itself. In the past there has been a practice, when charging corporations, not to charge the particular officers and directors. In recent cases, however, where corporations have disappeared by surrender of charter or amalgamation, it has been decided to proceed against the officials of such corporations who were concerned in the offence. Also, with relatively few exceptions, counsel have recommended that corporations only be charged.
Since requests for opinions normally ask who should be charged as principals, and in conspiracy cases named as co-conspirators, the usual answer to a question of this nature is that the parties prosecuted are those in accordance with the recommendation of counsel. Quite apart from any reluctance there may be to recommend prosecution of individuals, there frequently are sound practical reasons for prosecuting corporations only; for example, evidence of a particular officer or official may be necessary in the prosecution and this would not be available to the prosecution if the individual were charged as a princi-
April 25, 1972

pal in the same indictment and, if his evidence were necessary, there would be little point in preferring a separate indictment against him. Also, a prohibition order is applicable not only to the corporation convicted but to its directors, officers, employees, servants and agents. Since it is a perpetual order, it applies to persons occupying such positions at any time the order is in force. Orders against individuals apply only to that individual, and if he is transferred from his position the order may be of no practical value-for example, if he is transferred from a line to a staff position.
Now, let us examine very briefly the proposed provision for double damages on conviction. This is a very unusual device which presumably appears to have been used in an effort to avoid impinging upon provincial powers. It does not confer any civil right of action for a breach of such a right. The Supreme Court of Canada in Direct Lumber Company Limited versus Western Plywood Company Limited 1962 S.C.R. 646 has held that the then Criminal Code sections 411 (l)(c) relating to conspiracy in restraint of trade and 412 (l)(a) and (2) relating to price discrimination give no cause of action in damages to a person alleging a breach of these sections by another. It would appear that the same holds true for the successor provisions, 32 (l)(b) and 34(l)(a), and (2) respectively, and the other paragraphs of these provisions of the Combines Investigation Act. There may, however, be a right of action for common law conspiracy and also a right of action in Quebec under the civil law, but these points were not dealt with by the court.
The analogy to section 159 of the Excise Act-not section 158 as stated in the explanatory notes-is not an apt one. Section 159 refers to recovering double the amount of the excise duty and licence fee which should have been paid, a definite and readily ascertainable amount. Likewise, section 652 of the Criminal Code, also referred to in the explanatory notes, provides for recovery by civil proceedings of a fine, penalty or forfeiture imposed by law which is not only definite and readily ascertainable but is of course different from damages. The practicability of the section proposed in the bill, I submit, appears to be open to question.
It should be remembered that section 55 of Bill C-256, to enact the Competition Act, which was introduced at the last session of parliament, provides that a person who has suffered loss or damage as a result of a violation of any of the criminal provisions or a breach of an order of the Competitive Practices Tribunal may recover double damages. Also, section 80 provides that at the time sentence is imposed following a conviction the court may order the accused to pay to a person injured by the offence double the damages suffered by such person. This is an alternative to civil proceedings. Bill C-256 is presently being revised and representations have been received with respect to these provisions.
Section 8 deals with the personal liability of corporations, officers and agents. This clause provides that, where a corporation has committed an offence under the Combines Investigation Act or has failed to comply with an order made under the act, any director, manager or officer of the corporation who does or fails to do, or
Combines Investigation Act
acquiesces or assents in, any act constituting an offence or any element of such act or neglect, is guilty of the offence personally and jointly with the corporation. As the explanatory note in the proposed bill states, the principle of this provision is already contained in section 38 (e) which applies to refusal to permit entry of premises and examination of documents and failure to file returns of information. This section was first enacted as part of section 22(1) of the Combines and Fair Prices Act of 1919 and in similar form has been in the present Combines Investigation Act since 1923. There does not appear to have been any debate whatever on the provision, and therefore no indication why it was made applicable only to the foregoing provisions and not to others of a similar nature such as failure to make and submit affidavits when required. There is no other provision of this nature in the Combines Investigation Act.
In Bill C-256, the Competition Act, subsection 73(7) deals with the liability of officers or directors, where offences against the criminal provisions have been committed by a company, as follows:
(7) Where a company has been convicted of an offence under this section
(a)	every director of the company, and
(b)	every officer, servant or agent of the company who was in
whole or in part responsible for the conduct of that part of the
business of the company that gave rise to the offence,
is a party to the offence unless he satisfies a court that he had no knowledge of any of the acts constituting the offence and could not reasonably be expected to have had such knowledge and that he exercised reasonable diligence to prevent the commission of such an offence.
This provision in its present form has been subject to strong objection as imposing too heavy an onus, and imposing the same responsibility upon directors as upon officers responsible for the day to day operations of the company. In the revision of the bill this provision is being considered in the light of these objections.
Thus, Mr. Speaker, since as much work has and is being done on the whole question of the combines legislation, I would suggest that the questions raised by the hon. member would be better considered in the context of the legislation itself rather than as a separate entity. It is fair to say that the subject of the Combines Investigation Act is one that touches on the very fabric of our commercial structure. As a result, I feel that we owe it to the business community to review it as it relates to business law as a whole and not as an isolated aspect of business.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO STRENGTHEN PENALTIES FOR OFFENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I should like to say that I agree with most of what the hon. member for Welland (Mr. Tolmie) has had to say on this bill, but I think he is going a little too far when he asks that we attempt to solve these problems by approving the proposed competition bill. While some of the things the hon. member had to say concerning the problem in the context of that bill may be all right, like so many other things that are proposed by this government the bill contains some provisions that would make the price too high to pay.
In reference to the remarks of the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow), the sponsor of the bill, I should like to point out that while it is regrettable that

April 25, 1972
Combines Investigation Act
companies do combine to the detriment of the public and there have to be laws and punishments to deter such combinations, the examples that he mentioned did not seem to indicate that there was very much recidivism involved.
The hon. member did not produce any examples which would indicate that a jail term, as proposed by this legislation, would ever have been imposed. He referred to the Goodyear Tire and Rubber Company having two convictions registered against it in one year, but I would suspect that the offences arose in the same time-frame or in more or less the same transaction. No examples were given of a company committing an offence, say in 1960, another in 1965 and another two or three years ago.
I think one of the biggest problems in this area lies in the fact that the government does not seem able to secure as many convictions as are probably needed. There are many examples of municipalities putting work out to tender where the bids have been identical. This indicates there is something wrong, if not in the administration of the law at least in the manner in which it is framed. I say that the law must be more efficiently administered or adjustments must be made to it. There does not seem to be any evidence of the same people committing the same type of offence over and over again, and therefore there does not seem to be the need to increase the statutory penalties as proposed in this bill.
It is interesting to note that the hon. member who proposed the bill seems to have a different attitude toward this area of the law than he and his party have toward other areas of the criminal law and punishment. I refer particularly to the area of capital punishment and offences against existing drug laws. I am not convinced that jail terms are much of a deterrent; perhaps they are even less so than the mere fact of a conviction registered against an accused person or corporation in the area of law under review.
I am more concerned with clause 7 of the bill than the rest of it, because that clause would appear to allow an injured person to share with the Crown an increased monetary penalty; it appears to propose a 50-50 split. What is much more important here, Mr. Speaker, is that the law be changed to follow the practice in the United States where private prosecutions or private actions are allowed against offenders or monopolists or people who combine to increase prices to the detriment of the public. It may be said that this is a provincial matter, but such actions take place in federal courts in the United States.
Our confederation is slightly more centralized than confederation in the United States, so I do not understand why this practice could not be adopted here. We would probably have much more efficient administration in this respect if private enterprise were given a chance to enforce the law and if provision were made for people who have suffered as a result of unlawful combinations to bring action on their own behalf and to be rewarded for doing so by being awarded double or triple damages. I think the social ill we are striving to cure would be eradicated sooner if this type of incentive were provided to private enterprise.

In summary, I would say that no evidence has been produced that people repeat the offences referred to in this bill and therefore what is proposed by way of jail term will not be put into force. There is no evidence that it is needed. If damage is done to members of the public, they should be allowed to bring action to recover the damage caused by illegal combinations.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO STRENGTHEN PENALTIES FOR OFFENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in addressing myself to Bill C-13 I think it would be fair to say, as has already been said, that it appears to be merely a repetition of similar bills introduced by the hon. member over the last number of years. It has not changed in its proposals in any substantial way, so arguments put forward in past debates which have refuted any possible usefulness and adequacy of the bill and its forerunners are clearly pertinent and applicable now.
I say this particularly in view of the comments made a short while ago by the parliamentary secretary, the hon. member for Welland (Mr. Tolmie). He has explained quite well, I believe, that this bill has no particular importance at this time because the whole question of combination law in Canada is under comprehensive review and has been since the introduction at the last session of Bill C-256. Business organizations and consumer groups have, I believe, had admirable opportunity to make their views known in regard to the provisions of Bill C-256, the so-called competition act. I believe they have done so both publicly and privately to the present minister and to his immediate predecessor and departmental officials.
Perhaps, however, it would be a good idea to restate some of the arguments put forward in past-debates against the hon. member's proposals. The gist of Bill C-13 is that it would be mandatory for the courts to impose a sentence of imprisonment on a representative or representatives of a corporate entity for a second or third offence under the Combines Investigation Act. On June 5, 1964, the Honourable Mr. Marvin Gelber pointed out that the Criminal Code then provided for the kind of penalties for which the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orli-kow) was asking. He quoted a decision of Mr. Justice Judson in the case of Direct Lumber Company, Limited v. Western Plywood, Limited in which the justice said that section 21 of the Criminal Code provided as follows:
(1) Every one is a party to an offence who
(a)	actually commits it,
(b)	does or omits to do anything for the purpose of aiding any
person to commit it, or
(c)	abets any person in committing it.
Mr. Gelber pointed out that this made redundant the bill then introduced by the hon. member.

speechtext:
May I refer again to the remarks of the hon. member for York-Scarborough in 1966. At that time he made the following further observations which are undoubtedly applicable today:
Surely the net which Bill C-30-
That was the bill's number in 1966.
-attempts to cast to make all directors liable is too broad. For instance, certain conscientious officers might actively seek to prevent breaches of the combines act by their company's policy and would take great care to avoid any participation in or condonation of illegal activities.
The hon. member, who is now Minister of Communications, proposed a little later in his speech that the government be more venturesome in this type of legislation. He said:
Now, Mr. Speaker, I think the government of Canada could be much more venturesome in attempting to provide some real deterrent in respect of a breach of the law in this field and in providing some protection for consumers. This is something which I do not think Bill C-30 accomplishes at all.
I think that these words also apply to Bill C-13. The hon. member went on to say:
I believe our principal concern should be the protection of the consumers. Under its powers in the field of trade and commerce this parliament should be able to enact legislation which would make it possible to impose a civil liability on offending companies under the Combines Investigation Act.
I think Bill C-30 tends to be impractical in the accomplishment of the aims which it seems to have. Its minimum penalty provisions are not consistent with the trend of thinking in the whole field of criminal law. I believe the remedy, in the field of a deterrent, lies in better trained judges and perhaps prosecutors. I feel this is an area which has been neglected and should be examined most carefully by the new Department of the Registrar General with a view to obtaining some recompense for consumers who have suffered damages as a result of offences under this act.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that this is precisely what the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, which absorbed the Registrar General's department, is now attempting to do. A couple of years later when the hon. member's bill came forward again as Bill C-27, the hon. member for Elgin (Mr. Stafford) spoke to it. That was on March 15, 1968, to be exact. The hon. member for Elgin said:
Few sections of our Criminal Code make such sentences mandatory. There are some, for offences such as theft from the mails. But there are reasons for laying down minimum sentences in such cases. Under the Combines Investigation Act these reasons do not exist. I feel the judge trying the case is in the best position to judge
Combines Investigation Act
what sentence should be awarded, according to the merits of each case.
There are many reasons for believing that the amendments put forward in this bill will not work. For example, charges are usually laid against corporations-and corporations cannot be imprisoned. The provisions of Bill C-27 would have no effect on the corporations themselves. Moreover officials change, and those concerned in a second offence might well have had no connection whatever with a previous offence. And if the directors or officials of a corporation had changed a judge would hardly be able to sentence them at the time of a second offence, as outlined by the hon. member for Winnipeg North.
Then again, an offence by a company which had previously been convicted might involve an entirely different product line, and a court might not consider that an offence involving a different product line from that of the first offence did, in fact, amount to a second offence. It can easily be seen that many difficulties would arise and that the law might be much worse if these amendments were agreed to.
I believe I have shown, Mr. Speaker, or should I say the past record has shown, that provisions similar to those of Bill C-13 standing in the hon. member's name have been thoroughly debated in the House on many occasions. The proposals of the hon. member's bill are certainly not substantially changed and have been answered quite adequately, at least to my satisfaction. Furthermore, one hon. member who spoke earlier outlined some of the proposals of the competition bill which will, I feel, cover quite adequately the principles which the hon. member for Winnipeg North has for so long attempted to have enacted into law.
Also, as has been said, the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs is treating this very far reaching legislation with the delicacy it merits by giving all groups who wish to comment an opportunity to do so. This can only have a beneficial effect on the ultimate legislation, to the advantage of business and consumers alike.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will not say that this subject does not need refreshing comment. The hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) has again brought forward the subject, and I do not object. He reminds me of an old-time socialist who has not kept up with events in the last few years and does not know what has happened to the corporate structure. In his mind, large corporations are like the robber baron entities of 1910. He has never tried to bring himself up to date on how corporations act, and so on. Let us ask, what is the purpose of this bill? Let me say that I am not an apologist for corporations.
In the field of corporations a great deal must be done by this government that has not been done, and by provincial governments. Both levels of government must enact measures in connection with corporate structures, since these structures by and large are not really fulfilling the functions they are supposed to fulfil. Directors do not give a darn about what is going on in the business; they want to make money on the stock exchange. Stock exchanges are vying one with another to be the centre of the great con game. Shareholders no longer seem to carry much weight and the officers who run the company are divorced from the directors in regard to responsibility. The entire corporate structure should be reformed.

April 25, 1972
Combines Investigation Act
However, this bill has absolutely nothing to do with that subject. I feel that the hon. member for Winnipeg North does not actually know how a corporate body functions. I wonder if he can tell us exactly how combines come into being. If he can bring forward evidence, I am sure the Department of Justice would be only too pleased to listen to it. That department would like to know exactly which people in which corporations make deals with people in other corporations, and so on.
Suppose, for a moment, this bill were enacted into law. Do you think for a moment that the directors or officers would ever make a decision? Do you know what they would say? speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Supply and Services

speechtext:
I remind the hon. member that despite his great plea against combines, he nevertheless favours monopolies as they exist in Saskatchewan. If an enterprise is nationalized-in other words, if there is no free competition-a monopoly is created. The hon. member supports that kind of monopoly; it is in line with his political convictions. In that kind of monopoly an industry is in the hands of very few people and there is no competition of any kind.
Let me put this to the hon. member. At the present time, a corporation guilty of acts which may tend to raise prices or result in a combine can be put out of existence. No individual can be put out of existence. If the court feels the crime is sufficiently important, and if the corporation has $5 million in the kitty or $5 million in assets, there is nothing to prevent the court from imposing a fine of $1 million for each day of every infraction, and that corporation is dead so far as business is concerned.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO STRENGTHEN PENALTIES FOR OFFENCES
speechtext: Have they ever done it?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Supply and Services
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO STRENGTHEN PENALTIES FOR OFFENCES
speechtext:
I said if the court thinks it is advisable, not if the hon. member thinks it is advisable. We hear a great many complaints about corporations being nasty, and everything else; but when it comes to jobs, the hon. member is the first to say corporations should not be firing but should be hiring more people. The hon. member cannot have it both ways.
If the hon. member presented a bill which contained constructive ideas about how the whole corporate structure can be improved-and I dare say it can be improved, even recognizing some of the American concepts which have been adopted in regard to corporations-I would support it. However, to say this bill will prevent combines is nonsense. Before any legislation or ideas are presented we should find out why we have this state of affairs. Why do corporations try to combine or maintain a certain price level? By and large business is still very competitive. A business, corporate or otherwise, does not like to get into a position where there is no competition because there is no room for growth. It is a matter of distribution.
In most cases where there is any evidence of an attempt to hold a firm price, such as for cement and concrete as the hon. member mentioned, it is because the structure for tendering has broken down. I have been involved in business. A great part of business is tendering. When submitting a tender to a municipality or a large group where the money is secure you tend to reduce your price below that which is profitable. Invariably there is a company or concern which has a big staff and they do not want to get rid of that staff. They decide to put in a low bid for a city contract because it is large, even though they will lose money. They will then be able to continue in business. When the next contract comes along they will be able to tender a higher price because someone else will be underbidding. Then before you know it, everybody is underbidding.
Many companies which have tried to fix prices have gone out of business even with the fixing of prices. Many large corporations such as Perini and McNamara have suffered a great deal under our system of tendering because it is presumed that every corporation or company that tenders a price is thinking of a regular, normal price with a profit mark-up. They are not; in many cases they are in desperate straits or want a contract for some other reason. They make bad decisions just as other people do, with the result that they tumble one after another.
There are many cases presently before the courts where municipalities are being sued by suppliers and labourers in order to make up the difference when a contract has gone down under the tendering system. In effect, what we now have is a faulty system of tendering. For that reason some corporations try to get together. They feel that since they are all going to go down, they should see if they can come to terms. An individual or a corporation might try it but if they are caught, they are dead. The question, is why did they do it?
Should we not be thinking of a different method of tendering? For example, in the construction business in Italy, the lowest tenderer does not necessarily get the contract; there is an arrangement by which a tender which is closest to the estimate orginally made by the department or municipality is successful. Other countries
April 25, 1972

have other methods. The construction industry in Canada and the United States has been examining this problem, trying to find a new method by which the most able and most responsible person will get a contract to sell goods and services. We have a problem, but it is not as vast as the hon. member makes out. If we are to do anything about this problem, this bill will certainly not do it.
The hon. member referred to a recent decision of the Quebec court in connection with a contempt of court charge. I would like to refresh his memory. There is a vast difference between a contempt of court decision and a decision under the combines act.

speechtext: I will in a moment. If there is a court order against an individual within a corporation not to do something, and he does it, he will receive exactly the same punishment. That is the decision of the Quebec court. That case concerned an individual who by his actions displayed contempt of court. If this type of conduct were allowed we would have anarchy. The hon. member cannot on any ground refer to that type of decision and say, "Look at what they are doing there. This is a corporation doing the same thing again." However, it is not doing the same thing again. If there was a court order applying to a corporation executive or officer, and it was disregarded and the officer showed contempt of court, he would receive exactly the same punishment or jail term as in the case in Quebec.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to speaK on the amendment submitted by the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis). We will readily sup-
Family Income Security Plan
port that amendment. I would like to be able to support also Bill C-170 introduced by the hon. minister. Unfortunately, I could not congratulate the hon. minister, although we are not against an increase in family allowances, we want them at all costs.
I for one have been asking an increase in family allowances since I was elected as a member of this House in 1962 and family allowances have remained at the same level since then. In fact, the family allowances program did not change so to speak, since its establishment in 1945, except for a few scraps given just before an election to meet families' needs, to get the people's votes. Yet the cost of living increased by almost 300 per cent and all the sectors of the economy followed that increase; Parliament members' emoluments were increased as well as public servants' salaries, judges emoluments and employees salaries, but family allowances were not. Therefore it is about time we do something about family allowances.
We welcome the amendment of the hon. member for York South because we are opposed to a selective family allowance system.
I would like to speak of the right of Canadians to share in the profits derived from the goods of the community at large, a right which every citizen has.
Every citizen in every country, Mr. Speaker, is entitled to a share of the profits derived from the productive capital. Everyone has to be granted this right. This is distributive justice. We talk of the just society. In order to have a just society, you have to distribute its profits. According to distributive justice, profits have to be distributed to the society mostly within a family allowance system.
The objective of distributive justice, Mr. Speaker, is to insure that everyone shares in the collective wealth, for there is a hierarchy in any well-organized group, precisely because of the existence of the group, whose members have to receive their fair share.
This life in society, Mr. Speaker, has allowed for the passing on from one generation to the next of acquired knowledge, of technical advances. In our modern world, family allowances in Canada are still paid, at present, in an outmoded way.
According to the provisions of Bill C-170, payment of family allowances will certainly be made again on the former basis, because no consideration has been given to the needs, rights and prerogatives of every citizen.
The main feature of this bill is that the principle of universality will be replaced by that of selectivity; in other words, we shall cease to pay benefits to children irrespective of family revenue and allocate the amounts thus recuperated to the more disadvantaged.
Will this famous Bill C-170 stand out as a victory or a step backwards? I am convinced that it is rather a step backwards, since the enactment of this bill would be detrimental to families. Our heritage, amassed and increased through successive generations, is being trampled on. Real capital constitute an important factor in contemporary society. If members of this society do not share in the fruits of this capital, in productivity increase or in this vast heritage, they very well deserve being branded as deprived citizens. They are defrauded and

dispossessed of their share of inheritance. They are being made outcasts. Distributive justice, Mr. Speaker, will consequently be vioated and brutalized.
This is the case today with family allowances and it is more blatant still, since it is an integral part of the economy of developed countries. This inequity is obvious to the naked eye if we look at the facts as they are and not through the lens of regulations. Such is also the case on a world-wide scale because the people of under-developed countries also belong to the human race.
But our planet and its resources, Mr. Speaker, have been intended for all mankind. Therefore, there is already a certain common wealth, a gift of our Maker, in which everyone should somehow share. We are toying with a fundamental right, that of family allowances. It is more than fundamental; it is a common right given to each member of our society.
Therefore, man as a reasonable being, derived from nature itself the fundamental right to make use of the material riches of the earth, although the practical implementation of this right is left to the human will and to the judicial structures of nations. A basic right is always vested and need not be subject to any other principle; it proceeds from the very nature of man. A basic right cannot be questioned; what we must seek is the most effective means of granting this right more easily in practice.
Any legitimate and perfectly adapted government must offer a choice to its people. It must, however, establish adequate methods of distributing the goods, either domestic or imported, which are available on its territory.
It is neither in an unlimited production nor in the impressive statistics of trade and commerce that one must look for the true image of the actual prosperity of a people. One needs only consider the standard of living of each and every family and individual to determine the adequacy of material possessions. But does this adequacy exist?
Mr. Speaker, the economic wealth of a country does not really consist in abundant goods, measured by a simple appraisal of their actual value, but rather in what such an abundance represents as an adequate material basis for the individual and proper development of its citizens.
If a fair distribution of goods is not or is only partly achieved, the real objective of the national economy would not be attained. However abundant the goods may be, the people are poor because they are deprived of them.
Even though such a fair distribution may be effectively and lastingly achieved, the people will become poor, despite the large amount of available goods. Besides, it is a wrong to say, in our country with its large production, real or potential, that some people's wealth makes others poor.
Mr. Speaker, the rich do not eat all the bread nor do they wear all the clothes. Neither do they keep for themselves all building materials that the country may produce. Some people are ill-fed, poorly dressed, badly housed, but not because the rich are rich. Part of the population is deprived of essential goods taken from

Paul's plate, to put something in Peter's empty plate. This does not help at all, when one knows that the larder is full.
Mr. Speaker, this is the ridiculous and disastrous situation we are in. We are against such a legislation that goes against principles or condones the unfair distribution of material goods among the people and the families. However, it is no substitute for civil authorities when it comes to choose formulas or enact nonsensical laws and regulations.
Bill C-170, Mr. Speaker, does not meet the needs of the people.
There are surely some defects that must be eradicated from our present form of capitalism, such as the concentration of wealth and the faulty distribution of its abundant production. But this does not entitle me to replace it with the economic and political formulas of the Communist regime with its tremendous criminal record.
One must be incurably blind not to see them or dishonest to excuse them.
In itself, it is easier to distribute than to produce, when artificial obstacles are not raised. These exist in the economy of wealth of capitalism. They are of a financial order, and nobody can deny it, since this is where governments at all levels are stumbling.
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-170 is a violation of familial liberty since it is aimed at a degrading control of income which, rightly so, belongs to the family. It is time for the government to give back other people's property. We should give to anyone the right to distributive justice through national family allowances based on facts and reality.
Mr. Speaker, the facts prove that each citizen is entitled to the necessities of life. When national product goes on increasing, the Canadian standard of living should also rise. Both guaranteed minimum income and guaranteed salary should exist. Trade unions are uttering all kinds of protests demanding guaranteed salaries for workers. Financiers gained recognition of a guaranteed right to interest on their money.
In our society, many properties are so guaranteed but we have not yet given any guarantee to Canadian families and children, so that our country may reach the highest level of affluence and that our population may increase, because we know that in view of our tremendous responsibilities resulting from national, provincial, municipal and educational debts there are not enough citizens to distribute these debts conveniently. We must increase our population at all cost. Are we going to do it by depriving Canadians of their inherent right to justice?
Already we are depriving the Canadian people of their main right, a right to life, to usufruct, to discharge of justice and to distribution of property hoarded over generations. All that property hoarded over generations belongs to the citizens of this country. We know that Canada's population is not large enough. We know that on account of our debts, we would need at least 50 million inhabitants.
Now, Mr. Speaker, everything has been done to restrict the size of our population, to prevent people from developing, to prevent citizens from being born in this country.
April 25, 1972

We should grant every newborn child a dividend of at least $1,000. We should offer a gift to each father on the birth of his child, since a child means much more than an animal.
This afternoon, we had discussions with representatives of l'Union des cultivateurs. We were told-and we knew it, since a legislation to that end was passed in the House- that the farmers were to receive a $5 dividend for each weanling, whatever the number of weanlings.
But, when human beings are concerned, their number has to be restricted. Family allowances are being limited. Family allowances are being withdrawn from those who build the country, from the most valuable workers in the country, those who build homes, work day and night, develop themselves and our national heritage as well, who indirectly strengthen our economy. We are taking away from them what they are entitled to, that is family allowances. Family allowances are being withdrawn from those who pay the largest share of taxes, who are the biggest consumers, for, devoting most of their time to construction, they are constantly buying all kinds of materials.
We should finance Canadian families since they are the largest consumers within our economy. The larger the family, the higher the consumption. And, at the present time, there are surplus products in our country. This year, we have produced goods worth $95 billion, yet we hardly used up $54 billion. There remain some $40 billion surplus production in warehouses, on counters, that were capitalized. Individuals will have capitalized about $7 billion and corporations $30-odd billion.
Some hon. members say, like the member for Montmorency (Mr. Laflamme) for instance did last Thursday: Where are you going to get the money? You ask for higher family allowances but you do not even wonder where you will find the money. They find it dreadful to grant an additional $150 million to the population for a most noble and endearing cause. If we had no families we would not need any government. If we had no families we would not need any institution. Institutions are set up to serve families.
So let us put the family allowances at the service of the family, at the service of the nation. Let us give the nation all the encouragement required. The finest, most social, most human investment should be found within the family, within society. We should not subsidize piglets only but human beings as well because they really constitute our society's capital.
And if this society is going to the dogs, where shall we go, Mr. Speaker? Certainly, we need to increase our population, and it is up to us to take the necessary measures. If we have a surplus production of about $40 billion, we can find there all the financial means to help our families, to contribute to their development and we can make available to them the technology we have. We can also help the schools, universities and citizens to develop intellectually and morally, fully, in a word, because we have all the resources needed.
Although we have a surplus proauction of $40 billion this year, 50 per cent of the population is unemployed and, therefore, does not share in the increase of the national assets. If we were to put all these citizens to work and the
Family Income Security Plan
necessary capital in the hands of our consumers, of our large families, of all those who have children, so that they may spend and consume more, there would be an upsurge in our economy. Our economy would develop more and these citizens could pay more in taxes and returns to the state, while at the present time the less we give to our society, the more our society declines and our institutions deteriorate.
Mr. Speaker, I beg the hon. members and especially the minister to open their eyes. I beseech the minister to discard this famous bill and to bring out something new which will insure the necessary well being of our people. Our people have needs which we are in a position to meet since we have the necessary resources. At present the resources benefit some 20 per cent of the population at the very time when 80 per cent of that same population has a great number of needs. Therefore we must organize our economy so as to meet those needs, and allow our society to expand further and our families to get bigger and bigger through aid and encouragement.
This bill will deprive those who work in order to give something to those who work less. Generally speaking, those who will produce an income will pay for the others although they are the ones who really work and who do not spare their efforts in order to give the economy the impetus it needs.
I urge once more the minister to thoroughly revise his bill, to introduce a social measure that will be fair for all families, because it is the national distribution of goods which is at stake here. National resources do not belong only to a few individuals, but to all members of the community. And if this distribution is not done as it should, it is unfair, antisocial, inhuman, and it will result in a class struggle, already more pronounced than we suppose it to be.
This must stop, because we are here in order to give justice. We shall do this through an honest administration. The one that the minister proposes to us is not honest, because it is contrary to natural law, according to which each and everyone is entitled to his share of the heritage.
If some people are better off than others, or if they owe any dues to the state, the income tax people will see to it that these are collected. Vast surpluses, if any, could thus be reached through a reasonable system of taxation and basic exemptions.
But to deprive families earning $7,000, $8,000 or $10,000 from the bare necessities of life when they have mortgage payments to meet and other debts to pay, amounts to depriving them of the aspiration to have more children. By so doing, we would deny them the most sacred and important right, that of raising a family.
Families should be given incentives in accordance with the available surplus in our society. A just society should distribute this surplus, and by means of family allowances, we are distributing the value increase of society to everyone and every family and to those really in need.
There is much to be said in respect of Bill C-170. Let me simply mention, at this point, that we are in favour of the

amendment moved by the New Democratic Party which partly reads as follows:
-legislation amending the Family Allowances Act and the Youth Allowances Act to provide for a substantial increase in the allowances paid thereunder, for continuing the principle of universality, and for related changes in the income tax legislation.
We strongly support that suggestion and we congratulate the leader of the New Democratic Party for having presented it and we shall vote for the proposed amendment to give justice to every citizen, to every Canadian family, to provide the family with the necessary development so that it may progress for the good of the nation and that we may be able someday to reduce our national debt.
If society does not grow larger, obligations will be heavier for the taxpayers. Therefore, all necessary encouragement must be given to the family, to a logical and Christian point of view, so that it may develop; our society must take headway. Therefore laws must be just and must enable the family to develop normally. Our legislation should enable the family to take advantage of progress and science. All we have should serve society instead of subduing it.
We would still have much to say but I will not go through all particulars because many other members will do so. We must at all costs give our families the development they need to provide for their maintenance, in so far as the land enables them to get what they need. Land never refused to produce. Right now we have nothing but troubles: too much wheat in the west, too much grain, too many products of all kinds. We have to put restrictions on everything, we have to pay subsidies to prevent citizens from producing.
We realize, for instance, that there is an egg surplus. We have too many products of all sorts to spare. Therefore, we are not faced with a production problem in this country, where we own a hundred times more resources than we need. We could therefore increase our production.
Nearly 35 p. 100 of our population is now unemployed, living at the, expense of this society, because we have too many products to spare, because we do not want to increase our production. Since Providence has blssed us with plenty, it is up to us to manage our resources in such a way that all our people may benefit from them. Instead of boarding this glut, let us distribute it. We live in a land of plenty and we are paying farmers to refrain from producing, and we do it in every way possible. Therefore, let the family enjoy its prime rights, the right to live, and the right to develop, fully and freely.

This bill is difficult to interpret, and I do not know how the lay person who has not had the advantage of being in parliament or who does not have the legal talents of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro) can understand it. They were so far behind in making unemployment insurance payments that in many cases people went hungry. Many of them have come to my office and complained. his remarks be on record. Let him tell us how many welfare recipients are in that position. I tell him right now that my figures are different from his. About 1,300,000 families now receiving family allowances will be cut off entirely. Yet this same group will be paying taxes to provide this crossword puzzle trickery of family allowances. As I said before, a couple with one child 12 years of age or under, earning $9,000 per year, will receive no family allowance. A couple with one child between 12 and 17 years old, earning $10,500 a year, will not receive any family allowance. There is also the group earning $7,500 a year and up, which does not make them rich in today's society. These people have families and they are also taxpayers, with all the implications that that carries. These people will receive less in family allowances than they are now.
I never did like the means test, Mr. Speaker. It tends to create stratas in society, the haves and the have-nots, the rich and the poor. The middle-class is being eliminated. Factory people, farmers and office workers are the backbone of this country. They are the people who buy goods and supplies and pay taxes. With inflation running at about 7 per cent in housing and food, these people are poor at $7,000 a year. They are poor at $8,000 and poor at $9,000, and they are being discriminated against.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I say that this bill must be changed radically. In some respects the Minister of National Health and Welfare is a reasonable man. I hope that in committee the bill will be changed radically in the way that is necessary. The money supply this year has been greatly increased. I know this is an election year and the government wants to inflate everything; it wants everything going well so that it can say to the people, "You never had it better." This year the money supply has been increased by 30 per cent. It was increased by 21 per cent last year. By and by, if inflation is not running wild, something will be radically wrong, Mr. Speaker.
The government keeps changing its policies and monkeying around with the system. True, they did a little better with the old age pension system when they introduced the guaranteed income supplement and the 2 per cent cost of living escalation feature. The people affected by this bill will not get a nickel to compensate for the effects of inflation; they will not get one cent extra. Inflation this year is likely to run at 5 per cent. Why does this bill not take inflation into account? With inflation running wild, salaries will go ever upward. Consequently, fewer and fewer people will qualify for benefits. The minister will find it hard to say, "This is your manna from heaven," because hardly anyone will qualify.
Also, think of the cost of the bureaucracy that will be necessary to run the program. The demeaning means test must be swept out, Mr. Speaker. An increasing number of wage earners will be disqualified from benefit because of the hungry hands of inflation. Surely an escalator clause to take care of the effects of inflation could be included in the bill. We must also consider, as I have said, the great
